explanation: At duration = t_c, the entire watershed contributes flow to the outlet simultaneously, which maximizes Q. If the storm is shorter than t_c, parts of the watershed that are farther away have not had time to contribute their runoff to the outlet. Even though a shorter storm has higher intensity (from the IDF curve), the reduced contributing area more than offsets it. The Rational Method specifically uses duration = t_c to capture the maximum peak. The choice that Q increases is partially true (shorter storms are more intense) but misses that not all area contributes. The choice that Q stays the same ignores the time dimension. The choice that Q doubles for every halving of duration has no physical basis.

statement: A detention pond receives a constant inflow of $I = 120\text{ cfs}$ during the peak of a storm. The pond outlet discharges $O = 45\text{ cfs}$. After $2\text{ hours}$, how much water has accumulated in the pond?
explanation: $I - O = \Delta S/\Delta t$, so $\Delta S/\Delta t = 120 - 45 = 75$ cfs $= 75$ ft$^3$/s. Over 2 hours: $\Delta S = 75 \times (2 \times 3600) = 75 \times 7200 = 540{,}000$ ft$^3$. You must convert hours to seconds because the flow rates are in cfs (ft$^3$ per second). The 75 cfs choice gives the storage rate but not the accumulated volume. The 864,000 ft$^3$ choice uses $I \times t$ without subtracting outflow ($120 \times 7200 = 864{,}000$). The 324,000 ft$^3$ choice uses $O \times t$ ($45 \times 7200 = 324{,}000$).

statement: An aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of $K = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$, a hydraulic gradient of $i = 0.01$, and an effective porosity of $n = 0.25$. A technician reports the groundwater velocity as $2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$. What error did the technician make?

choices.text: The technician multiplied by porosity instead of dividing, making the answer too small
The technician reported the Darcy velocity ($q = Ki$) instead of the seepage velocity ($v = q/n$), which is 4 times larger
The technician used the correct formula but forgot to square the gradient
There is no error — this is the correct seepage velocity

explanation: Darcy velocity: $q = Ki = 2 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.01 = 2 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s. That is what the technician reported. But the actual seepage velocity is $v = q/n = 2 \times 10^{-6}/0.25 = 8 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s, which is 4 times larger. The Darcy velocity treats the entire cross-section as if water flows through all of it, but water only moves through the pore spaces. Dividing by porosity corrects for this. The "multiplied by porosity" choice describes multiplying by $n$, which would give an even smaller value ($5 \times 10^{-7}$). The "forgot to square the gradient" choice has no basis. The "no error" choice is wrong because $2 \times 10^{-6}$ is the Darcy velocity, not the seepage velocity.

statement: A well pumps from an unconfined aquifer using Dupuit's formula: $Q = \pi K(h_2^2 - h_1^2)/\ln(r_2/r_1)$. A student mistakenly applies the Thiem equation (linear $h$) instead. Compared to the correct answer, the student's computed $Q$ will be:

choices.text: Too high, because using linear heads overestimates the driving force
Too low, because $(h_2 - h_1) < (h_2^2 - h_1^2)/h_{avg}$ when the drawdown is large relative to the saturated thickness
The same, because both formulas give identical results
It depends only on whether $r_1 < r_2$ or $r_1 > r_2$

explanation: Dupuit uses $h^2$ differences: $h_2^2 - h_1^2 = (h_2 + h_1)(h_2 - h_1)$. The Thiem equation uses $h_2 - h_1$. The Dupuit formula effectively multiplies the head difference by the sum of the heads $(h_2 + h_1)$ (twice the average saturated thickness), which accounts for the fact that the flow area decreases as the water table drops near the well. Using linear $h$ underestimates this effect, giving a lower $Q$. The two formulas only agree when drawdown is very small compared to the total saturated thickness. The "too high" choice reverses the direction. The "both formulas give identical results" choice is wrong for unconfined aquifers. The "depends only on whether $r_1 < r_2$" choice has no physical basis.

statement: A wastewater sample has an ultimate BOD of $L_0 = 250\text{ mg/L}$ and a decay rate of $k = 0.23\text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the BOD exerted at day 3 ($BOD_3$)?
explanation: $BOD_3 = L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) = 250(1 - e^{-0.23 \times 3}) = 250(1 - e^{-0.69}) = 250(1 - 0.502) = 250 \times 0.498 = 125$ mg/L. About half the ultimate BOD has been exerted by day 3. The 250 mg/L choice gives the ultimate BOD, not the 3-day value. The 63 mg/L choice is roughly $BOD_1$ (one-day exertion). The 188 mg/L choice is closer to the $BOD_5$ range, not $BOD_3$.

statement: In the Streeter-Phelps dissolved oxygen sag model, the critical point (minimum DO) occurs where:

choices.text: The BOD has been completely consumed
The rate of deoxygenation (BOD consumption) equals the rate of reaeration from the atmosphere
The stream velocity reaches its minimum value

explanation: The DO sag curve has two competing processes: deoxygenation (organisms consuming oxygen as they decompose BOD) and reaeration (atmospheric oxygen dissolving into the water). Upstream of the critical point, deoxygenation dominates and DO drops. At the critical point, the two rates are exactly equal — DO stops dropping. Downstream of it, reaeration dominates and DO recovers. The "BOD completely consumed" choice is wrong because significant BOD may remain at the critical point. The "DO reaches zero" choice is wrong because DO rarely reaches zero in practice. The "minimum stream velocity" choice confuses velocity with the oxygen balance.

statement: A secondary clarifier treats a flow of $Q = 1.5\text{ MGD}$. The tank is circular with a diameter of $50\text{ ft}$. What is the overflow rate?
explanation: Overflow rate $= Q/A$. $A = \pi(50)^2/4 = 1{,}963$ ft$^2$. $Q = 1.5$ MGD $= 1{,}500{,}000$ gpd. $v_o = 1{,}500{,}000/1{,}963 = 764$ gpd/ft$^2$. This falls within the typical range for secondary clarifiers (400--800 gpd/ft$^2$). The 1{,}528 distractor divides $Q$ by half the surface area. The 382 distractor halves the correct overflow rate. The 30{,}000 distractor forgets to square the diameter in the area formula (uses $A \propto D$ instead of $D^2$).

statement: A settling basin has an overflow rate of $v_o = 600\text{ gpd/ft}^2$. Particle A has a settling velocity of $800\text{ gpd/ft}^2$ and Particle B has a settling velocity of $400\text{ gpd/ft}^2$. Which particles are removed?

choices.text: Both particles are completely removed because both are heavier than water
Particle A is completely removed; Particle B is only partially removed
Neither particle is removed because the overflow rate is positive
Particle B is completely removed; Particle A is only partially removed

explanation: The overflow rate acts as a threshold: any particle with $v_s > v_o$ will settle to the bottom before being carried out, so it is completely removed. Particle A: $v_s = 800 > 600$, so it settles faster than the upward flow velocity and is fully captured. Particle B: $v_s = 400 < 600$, so some of these particles will be carried over the weir. The fraction removed is roughly $v_s/v_o = 400/600 = 67\%$. The "both completely removed" choice ignores the overflow rate criterion. The "neither removed" choice misunderstands what overflow rate means. The "B removed, A partial" choice reverses the comparison.

statement: An aeration basin treats $Q = 5{,}000\text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ of wastewater with influent BOD $S_0 = 180\text{ mg/L}$. The basin volume is $V = 3{,}000\text{ m}^3$ and MLSS is $X_A = 2{,}500\text{ mg/L}$. What is the food-to-microorganism (F:M) ratio?
explanation: $F{:}M = Q \times S_0/(V \times X_A) = (5{,}000 \times 180)/(3{,}000 \times 2{,}500) = 900{,}000/7{,}500{,}000 = 0.12$ day$^{-1}$. The mg/L units cancel between $S_0$ and $X_A$, leaving m$^3$/day divided by m$^3$, which gives day$^{-1}$. This F:M is below the conventional range (0.2--0.4), suggesting extended aeration. The $1.20\text{ day}^{-1}$ choice inverts some terms. The $0.30\text{ day}^{-1}$ choice divides only by $V$ (ignores $X_A$). The $0.036\text{ day}^{-1}$ choice squares the volume in the denominator.

statement: An activated sludge plant operator reports an SRT ($\theta_c$) of $8\text{ hours}$ and an HRT ($\theta$) of $10\text{ days}$. Is this plausible?

choices.text: No — SRT is always much longer than HRT. The values are likely swapped.
Yes — SRT can be shorter than HRT if the sludge is wasted rapidly
Yes — SRT and HRT are independent parameters that can take any values
No — SRT and HRT must always be equal in a properly designed system

explanation: SRT (solids residence time) measures how long bacteria stay in the system — typically 4--15 days for conventional activated sludge. HRT (hydraulic residence time) measures how long water stays in the aeration basin — typically 4--8 hours. SRT is always much longer than HRT because we recycle the sludge (solids) back to the aeration basin, keeping the bacteria in the system far longer than the water. The reported values ($\theta_c = 8$ hr, $\theta = 10$ days) are clearly swapped. The "Yes — SRT can be shorter than HRT if the sludge is wasted rapidly" choice is wrong because rapid wasting still gives SRT of at least a few days. The "SRT and HRT are independent parameters" choice ignores the physical constraint that sludge recycle makes SRT $>$ HRT. The "SRT and HRT must always be equal" choice is wrong because they are never equal in practice.

statement: A rapid sand filter bed measures $24\text{ ft}$ by $12\text{ ft}$ and treats a flow of $Q = 1{,}728\text{ gpm}$. What is the filtration (loading) rate?
explanation: Filtration rate = Q/A_plan. Area = 24 × 12 = 288 ft². v_s = 1,728/288 = 6.0 gpm/ft², within the typical rapid-sand range of 2--10 gpm/ft². The 3.0 gpm/ft² choice doubles the area (1,728/576). The 0.17 gpm/ft² choice inverts the ratio (288/1,728). The 60 gpm/ft² choice drops a zero.

statement: Water with a chlorine demand of $1.8\text{ mg/L}$ must be dosed to leave a free residual of $0.5\text{ mg/L}$. For a flow of $Q = 2.0\text{ MGD}$, what is the chlorine feed rate? (Use $\text{lb/day} = \text{mg/L} \times \text{MGD} \times 8.34$.)
explanation: Dose = demand + residual = 1.8 + 0.5 = 2.3 mg/L. Feed rate = 2.3 × 2.0 × 8.34 = 38.4 lb/day. The 30.0 lb/day choice mis-scales the product without the proper 8.34 factor. The 15.0 lb/day choice roughly halves it. The 21.7 lb/day choice uses only the demand (1.8) × flow × 8.34, forgetting the 0.5 residual.

statement: A groundwater sample contains $\text{Ca}^{2+} = 70\text{ mg/L}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+} = 20\text{ mg/L}$. Using equivalent weights of $20$ (Ca²⁺) and $12.15$ (Mg²⁺), what is the total hardness as CaCO₃?
explanation: Convert each ion by 50/EW. Ca: 70 × 2.5 = 175. Mg: 20 × (50/12.15) = 20 × 4.12 = 82. Total = 175 + 82 = 257 mg/L as CaCO₃ (very hard). The 90 mg/L option adds raw ion values (70 + 20). The 175 mg/L option counts only calcium. The 200 mg/L option is a partial conversion.

statement: A pump delivers $Q = 0.08\text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ against a head of $H = 25\text{ m}$ at an efficiency of $\eta = 0.80$. What brake power is required? (Use $\rho g = 9{,}810\text{ N/m}^3$.)
explanation: Fluid power = γQH = 9,810 × 0.08 × 25 = 19,620 W ≈ 19.6 kW. Brake power = 19.6/0.80 = 24.5 kW. The 19.6 kW option is fluid power (no efficiency applied). The 15.7 kW option multiplies by 0.80 instead of dividing. The 30.7 kW option applies the efficiency twice.

statement: Water flows at $Q = 20\,\text{m}^3\text{/s}$ in a rectangular channel $B = 4\,\text{m}$ wide at a depth of $y = 2.5\,\text{m}$. What is the specific energy of the flow?
explanation: Specific energy is depth plus velocity head: $E = y + v^2/(2g)$. First the velocity: $v = Q/A = 20/(4 \times 2.5) = 2.0$ m/s. Then $v^2/(2g) = 4/(2 \times 9.81) = 0.204$ m. $E = 2.5 + 0.204 = 2.70$ m. The 2.50 m choice reports only the depth, forgetting the velocity head entirely. The 2.91 m choice uses $v^2/g$ (omitting the factor of 2 in the velocity head). The 0.20 m choice reports only the velocity head, forgetting to add the depth.

statement: A hydraulic jump in a wide rectangular channel has an upstream (supercritical) depth of $y_1 = 0.5\,\text{m}$ and a downstream (subcritical) conjugate depth of $y_2 = 2.5\,\text{m}$. What is the energy lost across the jump?
explanation: When both conjugate depths are known, the energy loss has a closed form: $\Delta E = (y_2 - y_1)^3/(4 y_1 y_2)$. $\Delta E = (2.5 - 0.5)^3/(4 \times 0.5 \times 2.5) = (2.0)^3/5.0 = 8/5 = 1.60$ m. The 6.40 m option omits the factor of 4 in the denominator: $(2.0)^3/(0.5 \times 2.5) = 6.40$. The 2.00 m option just reports the depth difference $y_2 - y_1 = 2.0$. The 4.00 m option drops $y_2$ from the denominator: $(2.0)^3/(4 \times 0.5) = 4.00$.

statement: A storm drain inlet must be sized for a peak design flow of $Q = 90\,\text{cfs}$. The contributing area has a runoff coefficient $C = 0.55$ and the design rainfall intensity is $I = 3.0\,\text{in./hr}$. Using the Rational Method, what drainage area does this represent?
explanation: Rearrange $Q = CIA$ to solve for area: $A = Q/(CI) = 90/(0.55 \times 3.0) = 90/1.65 = 54.5$ acres. The Rational Method units work out directly (1 acre-in./hr $\approx$ 1 cfs), so no conversion is needed. The 16.5-acre choice multiplies by $C$ instead of dividing: $QC/I = 90(0.55)/3.0 = 16.5$. The 30.0-acre choice ignores $C$ entirely: $Q/I = 90/3.0 = 30$. The 163.6-acre choice forgets the intensity: $Q/C = 90/0.55 = 163.6$.

statement: A storm produces a direct runoff volume of $1{,}500\,\text{acre-ft}$ from a watershed with a drainage area of $6{,}000\,\text{acres}$. What is the equivalent depth of direct runoff over the watershed?
explanation: Runoff depth is volume divided by area, then converted to inches. In consistent units, depth $= V/A = 1{,}500/6{,}000 = 0.25$ ft. Convert to inches: $0.25 \times 12 = 3.0$ in. The acre cancels between acre-ft and acres, leaving feet, which you multiply by 12. The 0.25 in. choice stops at 0.25 ft but mislabels it as inches (forgot the factor of 12). The 6.0 in. choice doubles the result by an arithmetic slip. The 36.0 in. choice multiplies by 12 twice (applies 144 instead of 12).

statement: Water seeps horizontally through a confined sand layer beneath a dam. The hydraulic conductivity is $K = 4 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m/s}$, the flow cross-section is $A = 300\,\text{m}^2$, and the head drops $6\,\text{m}$ over a flow path length of $120\,\text{m}$. What is the seepage discharge in cubic meters per day?
explanation: Darcy's law gives the volumetric flow: $Q = KAi$, where the gradient is $i = dh/L = 6/120 = 0.05$. So $Q = (4 \times 10^{-5})(300)(0.05) = 6.0 \times 10^{-4}$ m$^3$/s. Convert to per day: $6.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 86{,}400 = 51.8$ m$^3$/day. The $0.17$ m$^3$/day choice forgets the cross-sectional area, using $Ki$ only (times 86,400). The $6{,}221$ m$^3$/day choice forgets to divide the head drop by the path length, using $i = 6$ instead of $0.05$, inflating $Q$ by 120 times. The $2.6$ m$^3$/day choice mishandles the area, dividing by it instead of multiplying.

statement: A wastewater sample has an ultimate BOD of $L_0 = 320\,\text{mg/L}$ and a decay rate of $k = 0.18\,\text{day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the BOD remaining (not yet exerted) after 4 days?
explanation: BOD remaining is the organic matter not yet decomposed: $L_t = L_0 e^{-kt} = 320\,e^{-0.18 \times 4} = 320\,e^{-0.72} = 320(0.487) = 155.8$ mg/L. Note the BOD exerted ($L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) = 164.2$) plus the remaining ($155.8$) sum to the ultimate $320$. The 164.2 mg/L choice gives the BOD exerted rather than remaining. The 57.6 mg/L choice applies $kt$ as a percentage ($0.18 \times 4 = 0.72$, then $320 \times 0.18 = 57.6$), a formula confusion. The 320 mg/L choice reports the ultimate BOD, as if no decay had occurred.

statement: A chlorine contact basin holds a free residual of $C = 2.0\,\text{mg/L}$, and the $10$th-percentile contact time is $t_{10} = 45\,\text{min}$. What disinfection CT value is achieved?
explanation: CT = C × t₁₀ = 2.0 × 45 = 90 mg·min/L. The 22.5 mg·min/L choice divides instead of multiplying (45/2). The 47 mg·min/L choice adds the two values (2 + 45). The 0.044 mg·min/L choice divides C by t₁₀ (2/45) rather than multiplying.

statement: A filter sand has an effective size $d_{10} = 0.50\,\text{mm}$ and $d_{60} = 0.75\,\text{mm}$. What is the uniformity coefficient of the media?
explanation: Uniformity coefficient UC = d₆₀/d₁₀ = 0.75/0.50 = 1.5. A lower UC means more uniform grain sizes. The 0.67 option inverts the ratio (d₁₀/d₆₀). The 1.25 option uses a wrong pairing. The 0.25 option subtracts the sizes.

statement: A wastewater plant receives total suspended solids of $220\,\text{mg/L}$ and must discharge at or below $30\,\text{mg/L}$. What TSS removal efficiency is required?
explanation: Efficiency = (in − out)/in = (220 − 30)/220 = 190/220 = 0.864 = 86.4%. The 13.6% choice is the fraction remaining (30/220). The 30% choice reports the effluent number as a percent. The 7.3% choice inverts the ratio.

statement: A pump must overcome a static lift of $18\,\text{m}$ plus friction and minor losses of $6.5\,\text{m}$ while delivering $Q = 0.030\,\text{m}^3\text{/s}$ at a pump efficiency of $\eta = 0.70$. What brake power is required? (Use $\rho g = 9{,}810\,\text{N/m}^3$.)
explanation: Total dynamic head = static + losses = 18 + 6.5 = 24.5 m. Fluid power = γQH = 9,810 × 0.030 × 24.5 = 7,210 W ≈ 7.2 kW. Brake power = 7.2/0.70 = 10.3 kW. The 7.2 kW option is the fluid power (no efficiency). The 5.3 kW option uses only the static lift (9,810 × 0.030 × 18 ≈ 5,300 W). The 5.0 kW option multiplies by 0.70 instead of dividing (7.2 × 0.70 ≈ 5.0).

statement: A planar truss has $m = 11$ members, $r = 3$ reaction components, and $j = 7$ joints. How is the structure classified?
explanation: For a plane truss: m + r = 11 + 3 = 14, and 2j = 2(7) = 14. Since m + r = 2j, the truss is stable and statically determinate. This means you can find all member forces and reactions using equilibrium equations alone. If m + r were greater than 2j, you would need compatibility equations (indeterminate). If less, the structure would be a mechanism.

statement: A portal frame consists of $m = 3$ members and $j = 4$ joints. The left base has a pin support and the right base has a fixed support. There are no internal hinges ($c = 0$). What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
explanation: For a plane frame: compare 3m + r to 3j + c. Reactions: pin = 2 components, fixed = 3 components, so r = 2 + 3 = 5. Then 3m + r = 3(3) + 5 = 14, and 3j + c = 3(4) + 0 = 12. Since 14 > 12, the frame is indeterminate, and the degree = 14 – 12 = 2. That means you need two compatibility equations beyond equilibrium to solve for all unknowns. The "0 (determinate)" choice would require 3m + r = 3j + c exactly. The "3 degrees" choice would happen if both supports were fixed (r = 6, giving 3(3)+6 = 15 vs 12 = 3 degrees).

statement: A planar truss has $m = 9$ members, $r = 3$ reaction components, and $j = 6$ joints. All three reaction components are vertical (parallel). Is the truss stable?
explanation: Numerically: m + r = 9 + 3 = 12, and 2j = 2(6) = 12. The equation says determinate. But the equation is a necessary condition, not sufficient. If all three reaction components are parallel (all vertical), the structure cannot resist any horizontal force — it slides sideways. This is called geometric instability. The truss is unstable even though the count checks out. Always verify that reactions are not all parallel or concurrent. The "stable and determinate" choice assumes the count alone guarantees stability — it does not.

statement: At joint A, a $500\text{ lb}$ vertical (downward) load is carried by two members: a horizontal member AB and a diagonal member AC oriented at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal. Using the method of joints, what is the force in diagonal AC?
explanation: Only the diagonal can resist the vertical load — the horizontal member has no vertical component. So $\sum F_y = 0$ gives $F_{AC}\sin 45^\circ = 500$, hence $F_{AC} = 500/0.707 = 707$ lb. The 500 lb choice forgets to divide by $\sin 45^\circ$. The 354 lb choice multiplies by $\sin 45^\circ$ instead of dividing.

statement: A parallel-chord truss has panel length $4\text{ m}$ and height $3\text{ m}$. The left support reaction is $30\text{ kN}$ (upward) and there are no loads within the first panel. Taking a vertical section through the first panel and summing moments about the top-chord joint at the far end of the panel, what is the force in the bottom chord?
explanation: Summing moments about the top joint kills the diagonal and the top chord (they pass through or are arms about that point), leaving only the bottom chord. The reaction acts $4\text{ m}$ horizontally from the moment center; the bottom chord acts at the $3\text{ m}$ height. So $30(4) = F_{BC}(3)$, giving $F_{BC} = 120/3 = 40\text{ kN}$ tension. The 120 kN option forgets to divide by the 3 m height.

statement: At an unloaded joint, three members meet: two are collinear (in a straight line through the joint) and the third comes in at an angle. No external load or reaction acts at this joint. What is the force in the angled (third) member?

choices.text: Equal to the force in the collinear members

explanation: Set up equilibrium perpendicular to the two collinear members. The two collinear members have no component in that perpendicular direction, and there's no external load — so the only force with a component there is the angled member, which must therefore be zero. This is the classic zero-force-member rule.
handbookRef: p. 97, Plane Truss: Method of Joints

statement: Using the unit-load method for a truss, $\delta = \sum nNL/AE$. For one member, the real force is $N = 50\text{ kN}$, the virtual (unit-load) force is $n = 0.5$, the length is $L = 4\text{ m}$, and $AE = 200{,}000\text{ kN}$. What is this member's contribution to the joint deflection?
explanation: Plug into $nNL/AE = (0.5)(50)(4)/200{,}000 = 100/200{,}000 = 0.0005\text{ m} = 0.5\text{ mm}$. The trap is units: $0.0005\text{ m}$ is $0.5\text{ mm}$, not $5\text{ mm}$ (the $5.0\text{ mm}$ choice) or $0.05\text{ mm}$ (the $0.05\text{ mm}$ choice).

statement: A simply supported beam of length $L = 6\text{ m}$ carries a central point load $P = 20\text{ kN}$. The flexural rigidity is $EI = 40{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$. What is the maximum deflection?
explanation: Central point load on a simple span uses $\delta = PL^3/48EI = 20(6^3)/(48 \times 40{,}000) = 4320/1{,}920{,}000 = 0.00225\text{ m} = 2.25\text{ mm}$. The 9 mm choice uses $PL^3/12EI$ by mistake; the 1.13 mm choice halves the answer.

statement: A cantilever beam of length $L = 3\text{ m}$ carries a point load $P = 10\text{ kN}$ at its free end. With $EI = 20{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$, what is the tip deflection?
explanation: End-loaded cantilever: $\delta = PL^3/3EI = 10(27)/(3 \times 20{,}000) = 270/60{,}000 = 0.0045\text{ m} = 4.5\text{ mm}$. The 2.25 mm distractor wrongly uses $PL^3/6EI$ (an erroneous denominator constant of 6 instead of 3); the 13.5 mm distractor drops the factor entirely and uses $PL^3/EI$.

statement: A propped cantilever beam is fixed at one end and supported on a roller at the other. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
explanation: Count reactions: the fixed end provides 3 (horizontal, vertical, moment) and the roller provides 1 (vertical), giving 4. A planar beam has 3 equilibrium equations, so $DSI = 4 - 3 = 1$ — indeterminate to the first degree. The "0" option would be a determinate beam (e.g., simply supported).

statement: A propped cantilever (fixed at one end, roller at the other) of length $L = 8\text{ m}$ carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 12\text{ kN/m}$. What is the reaction at the propped (roller) end?
explanation: The standard propped-cantilever result for a UDL gives the prop (roller) reaction $R = 3wL/8 = 3(12)(8)/8 = 36\text{ kN}$. The 48 kN choice is the simple-span half-load $wL/2$, ignoring that the fixed end takes more (it carries 60 kN). The 24 kN choice uses $wL/4$.

statement: A beam fixed at both ends spans $L = 6\text{ m}$ and carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 10\text{ kN/m}$. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support?
explanation: Fixed-fixed beam under UDL: the fixed-end moment is $wL^2/12 = 10(6^2)/12 = 360/12 = 30\text{ kN·m}$. The 45 kN·m choice uses the simple-span midspan moment $wL^2/8$ by mistake — that's the wrong formula for a fixed end.

statement: A beam supports a dead load of $D = 20 \text{ kips}$ and a floor live load of $L = 40 \text{ kips}$. What is the factored load using LRFD Combination 2 ($1.2D + 1.6L$)?
explanation: 1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(20) + 1.6(40) = 24 + 64 = 88 kips. This is the most common LRFD combination for gravity loading. The 60 kips option is the unfactored sum D + L. The 96 kips option applies 1.6 to both D and L, which is wrong — dead load gets a lower factor (1.2) because it is more predictable. The 84 kips option might come from using wrong factors like 1.4D + L.

statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 24 \text{ ft}$. A single concentrated load $P = 12 \text{ kips}$ can be placed anywhere on the beam. Using the influence line for shear at a section 6 ft from the left support, what is the maximum positive shear at that section?
explanation: The IL for positive shear at a section has its maximum ordinate just to the right of the section. At a = 6 ft from the left support of a span L = 24 ft, the IL ordinate just to the right = 1 – a/L = 1 – 6/24 = 0.75. Maximum positive shear = P × 0.75 = 12 × 0.75 = 9.0 kips. The 12 kips choice assumes the full load becomes shear. The 3 kips choice uses the negative ordinate a/L = 0.25. The 6 kips choice is half the load.

statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 30 \text{ ft}$. A concentrated load of $P = 20 \text{ kips}$ moves across the beam. What is the maximum bending moment at midspan?
explanation: The IL for moment at midspan is a triangle with peak ordinate = L/4 at midspan. Peak ordinate = 30/4 = 7.5 ft. Maximum moment = P × (L/4) = 20 × 7.5 = 150 kip-ft. This occurs when the load is placed directly at midspan. The 300 kip-ft option might come from PL/2, confusing moment with the reaction formula. The 75 kip-ft option halves the correct answer. The 600 kip-ft option uses P × L = 20 × 30.

statement: A concrete column is $18 \text{ in.} \times 18 \text{ in.}$ with 4 #8 bars (each $A_b = 0.79 \text{ in}^2$). Is the reinforcement ratio within ACI limits?
explanation: A_st = 4 × 0.79 = 3.16 in². A_g = 18 × 18 = 324 in². ρ_g = 3.16/324 = 0.00975 = 0.975%. ACI requires 0.01 ≤ ρ_g ≤ 0.08 (1% to 8%). Since 0.975% < 1%, the reinforcement is below the minimum. This means the column has insufficient steel to prevent a sudden brittle failure under combined axial load and bending. The fix is to add more bars or use larger bars. The "Yes — within the 1% to 8% range" choice would require ρ_g ≥ 0.01. The "At the exact minimum of 1%" choice would require exactly 0.01.

statement: A W-shape steel beam has $Z_x = 120 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. The beam has full lateral bracing. What is the LRFD design flexural strength $\phi_b M_n$?
explanation: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 120 = 6{,}000$ kip-in $= 500$ kip-ft. Then $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 500 = 450$ kip-ft. The 500 kip-ft choice is the nominal capacity without the $\phi$ factor. The 299 kip-ft choice is the ASD allowable: $M_p/\Omega_b = 500/1.67 = 299$ — a common trap if you mix up LRFD and ASD. The 333 kip-ft choice comes from using $\phi = 2/3$ incorrectly.

statement: A steel column has an effective length $KL = 15 \text{ ft}$ and a weak-axis radius of gyration $r_y = 1.91 \text{ in.}$ What is the slenderness ratio $KL/r_y$?
explanation: First convert $KL$ to inches: $15 \times 12 = 180$ in. Then $KL/r_y = 180/1.91 = 94.2 \approx 94$. The choice 180 is $KL$ in inches without dividing by $r$. The choice 31 uses the strong-axis $r_x$ (if $r_x = 5.85$ in., then $180/5.85 = 30.8 \approx 31$). The choice 7.9 reverses the fraction ($r/KL \times 1000$). Always convert feet to inches before dividing by $r$.

statement: A steel column has $KL/r = 60$ and a cross-sectional area $A_g = 15.0 \text{ in}^2$. Using $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ and AISC Table 4-14 (which gives $\phi_c F_{cr} = 34.6 \text{ ksi}$ at $KL/r = 60$), what is the LRFD design compressive strength?
explanation: $\phi_c P_n = \phi_c F_{cr} \times A_g = 34.6 \times 15.0 = 519$ kips. That is the total design compressive strength after buckling reduction and safety factor. The 750 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 50 \times 15 = 750$, which ignores buckling entirely — this would only be correct for a zero-length column. The 345 kips choice might come from an incorrect table lookup. The 675 kips choice applies $\phi_c = 0.90$ to the gross yield: $0.90 \times 750 = 675$, still ignoring buckling.

statement: Two columns use the same W-shape ($r_y = 2.0 \text{ in.}$). Column A has an unbraced length of $12 \text{ ft}$ with pin-pin supports ($K = 1.0$). Column B has an unbraced length of $18 \text{ ft}$ with fixed-pin supports ($K = 0.80$). Which column has the higher slenderness ratio?
explanation: Column A: $KL/r = (1.0 \times 12 \times 12)/2.0 = 144/2.0 = 72$. Column B: $KL/r = (0.80 \times 18 \times 12)/2.0 = 172.8/2.0 = 86.4 \approx 86$. Column B has the higher $KL/r$ despite having a lower $K$ factor, because its physical length is much longer. Higher $KL/r$ means lower $\phi_c F_{cr}$ and therefore lower design strength. The choice "Column A because $K = 1.0 > 0.80$" is the trap — a lower $K$ factor helps, but it does not always compensate for a much longer column. You must compute the actual $KL/r$ to compare.

statement: A flat bar ($1/2 \text{ in.} \times 6 \text{ in.}$) is used as a tension member with $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$ and $F_u = 58 \text{ ksi}$. There are no bolt holes. What is the LRFD design tensile strength for yielding?
explanation: $A_g = 0.5 \times 6 = 3.0$ in$^2$. For yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times F_y \times A_g = 0.90 \times 36 \times 3.0 = 97.2 \approx 97$ kips. The 108 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 108$ without the $\phi$ factor. The 174 kips choice uses $F_u$ instead of $F_y$ with no $\phi$ factor: $174 = F_u \times A_g = 58 \times 3.0$. The 131 kips choice uses $\phi = 0.75$ with $F_u$: $0.75 \times 58 \times 3.0 = 130.5 \approx 131$ — that is the rupture check, not yielding.

statement: A plate tension member is $1/2 \text{ in.}$ thick and $10 \text{ in.}$ wide. Two $7/8 \text{-in.}$ diameter bolts are placed at the same cross-section (side by side). What is the net area $A_n$?
explanation: For each bolt hole, subtract $(d_b + 1/8")$ from the gross width: $7/8 + 1/8 = 1.0$ in. per hole. With 2 holes: $A_n = [10 - 2(1.0)] \times 0.5 = 8.0 \times 0.5 = 4.00$ in$^2$. The $1/8"$ comes from $1/16"$ hole clearance $+ 1/16"$ drilling damage. The $4.13 \text{ in}^2$ option subtracts only $d_b = 0.875$ per hole without the extra $1/8"$: $[10 - 2(0.875)] \times 0.5 = 4.125$. The $5.00 \text{ in}^2$ option is the gross area with no deductions. The $4.06 \text{ in}^2$ option adds only $1/16"$ instead of $1/8"$ to each bolt diameter.

statement: A planar truss has 9 members, 6 joints, and 3 external reactions. Is the truss statically determinate?

choices.text: No, it is statically indeterminate by 2 degrees
No, it is statically indeterminate by 1 degree

explanation: For a truss: $m + r = 2j$ for determinate. Here: $9 + 3 = 12$, and $2(6) = 12$. Since $m + r = 2j$, the truss is statically determinate. If $m + r > 2j$, it is indeterminate. If $m + r < 2j$, it is unstable.

statement: A structure is externally stable but has $m + r > 2j$. This means the structure is:
explanation: When $m + r > 2j$, there are more unknowns than equilibrium equations. The structure has redundant members or supports -- it is statically indeterminate. You would need compatibility equations in addition to equilibrium to solve it. The degree of indeterminacy is $(m + r) - 2j$.

statement: A plane frame has $m = 5$ members, $j = 6$ joints, and two internal hinges ($c = 2$). The supports consist of two pin supports and one roller. What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
explanation: For frames, compare $3m + r$ to $3j + c$. Reactions: two pins give $2 + 2 = 4$, one roller gives 1, so $r = 5$. Then $3m + r = 3(5) + 5 = 20$, and $3j + c = 3(6) + 2 = 20$. Since $20 = 20$, the frame is statically determinate (degree = 0). Each internal hinge provides one extra condition equation, which reduces the degree of indeterminacy. Without those two hinges, the frame would be indeterminate to the 2nd degree.

statement: A planar truss satisfies $m + r > 2j$. However, all external reactions pass through a single point. What is the correct classification?

choices.text: Unstable — concurrent reactions cannot maintain equilibrium
Indeterminate unless a moment equation is added

explanation: The numerical count $m + r > 2j$ suggests indeterminacy, but that equation is only a necessary condition for stability, not a sufficient one. If all reaction lines of action pass through a single point (concurrent reactions), the structure cannot resist a moment about that point. Apply the moment equilibrium equation $\Sigma M = 0$ at that point and you get 0 = something nonzero, which is impossible. The structure is geometrically unstable regardless of how many extra members or reactions it has. Always check the arrangement of reactions, not just the count.

statement: A roof beam supports $D = 15 \text{ kips}$ and a roof live load $L_r = 20 \text{ kips}$. No floor live load, snow, wind, or seismic. What is the factored load using LRFD Combination 3 ($1.2D + 1.6L_r$)?
explanation: Combination 3 with only roof live load active is $1.2D + 1.6L_r = 1.2(15) + 1.6(20) = 18 + 32 = 50$ kips. The 35 kips choice is the unfactored sum $D + L_r = 15 + 20$. The 21 kips choice is Combination 1: $1.4D = 1.4(15) = 21$. The 56 kips choice comes from applying 1.6 to both loads: $1.6(15) + 1.6(20) = 56$, but dead load gets 1.2, not 1.6.

statement: In LRFD, why does dead load receive a lower load factor (1.2) than live load (1.6)?

choices.text: Dead load is more predictable; live load has greater statistical variability
Dead load is always smaller than live load
ASCE 7 assigns factors based on load duration, not uncertainty
Dead load only acts during construction, so it needs a smaller factor

explanation: Load factors in LRFD reflect the uncertainty in predicting each load magnitude. Dead load (self-weight of structure, permanent fixtures) can be calculated accurately from material densities and dimensions, so its variability is low — hence a 1.2 factor. Live load (people, furniture, stored goods) is much harder to predict and varies widely over a building's life, so it gets the larger 1.6 factor. The "dead load is always smaller than live load" choice is wrong because dead load can easily exceed live load in some structures. The "factors based on load duration" choice confuses duration with uncertainty. The "dead load only acts during construction" choice is incorrect — dead load acts permanently, not just during construction.

statement: A column supports $D = 50 \text{ kips}$, $L = 30 \text{ kips}$, and $S = 60 \text{ kips}$. In LRFD Combination 2, $L$ gets the 1.6 factor. In Combination 3, $S$ gets the 1.6 factor. Which combination controls and why?

choices.text: Combination 1 ($70 \text{ kips}$) — dead load alone is the critical case
Combination 2 ($138 \text{ kips}$) — Combination 2 always controls for gravity loading
Combination 3 ($186 \text{ kips}$) — snow dominates floor live load, so the 1.6 factor on $S$ produces a larger total
They are equal because $D$ has the same factor in both

explanation: Combo 2: $1.2(50) + 1.6(30) + 0.5(60) = 60 + 48 + 30 = 138$ kips. Combo 3: $1.2(50) + 1.6(60) + 1.0(30) = 60 + 96 + 30 = 186$ kips. Combo 3 controls at 186 kips because snow ($S = 60$) is much larger than floor live load ($L = 30$), so putting the 1.6 factor on snow amplifies the dominant transient load. The Combination 2 (138 kips) choice assumes Combo 2 always governs — that is only true when floor live load exceeds snow. You must always evaluate multiple combinations and pick the largest.

statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 20 \text{ ft}$. Using the influence line for the left reaction $R_A$, what is the IL ordinate when a unit load is placed $5 \text{ ft}$ from the left support?
explanation: The influence line ordinate for the left reaction at position $x$ from the left support is $(L - x)/L$. At $x = 5$ ft: $(20 - 5)/20 = 15/20 = 0.75$. This means when a unit load sits 5 ft from A, the left reaction carries 75% of it. The 0.25 choice uses $x/L$ instead of $(L - x)/L$ -- that would be the reaction at B. The 1.0 choice is the ordinate when the load is directly over A ($x = 0$).

statement: For a simply supported beam, where does the influence line for bending moment at a section located at distance $a$ from the left support have its maximum ordinate?

choices.text: Directly at the section, with ordinate $a(L - a)/L$
At the left support, with ordinate 1.0
At the right support, with ordinate 1.0

explanation: The influence line for bending moment at a section is triangular. It goes from 0 at both supports to a peak at the section itself. The peak ordinate is $a(L - a)/L$. This means to produce the maximum moment at that section, you place the load directly at the section. The midspan-ordinate choice ($L/4$) is only correct when the section happens to be at midspan ($a = L/2$, giving $L/4$). The two support choices (ordinate 1.0 at a support) describe the reaction influence line, not the moment influence line.

statement: A simply supported beam has a section at the quarter point ($a = L/4$). The influence line for shear at that section has a positive ordinate of $+0.75$ just to the right and a negative ordinate of $-0.25$ just to the left. To maximize the positive shear using a single moving concentrated load, where should the load be placed?

choices.text: Just to the left of the section
Just to the right of the section

explanation: The IL for shear at a section jumps by 1.0 at the section. On the right side of the section, the ordinate is positive and maximum just to the right of the cut ($+0.75$), decreasing linearly to 0 at the right support. On the left side, ordinates are negative. To maximize the positive shear, place the load where the positive ordinate is largest — that is just to the right of the section. Placing the load at midspan gives a smaller positive ordinate (the IL decreases linearly from the section to the right support). Placing it just to the left gives the maximum negative shear ($-0.25$), not positive. At the right support, the ordinate is 0.

statement: A singly reinforced beam has $b = 14 \text{ in.}$, $d = 22 \text{ in.}$, $A_s = 4.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_c' = 3 \text{ ksi}$. What is the stress block depth $a$?
explanation: $a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f_c' b) = 4.00 \times 60 / (0.85 \times 3 \times 14) = 240/35.7 = 6.72$ in. The 5.71 in. choice could come from $A_s f_y / (f_c' b) = 240/42 = 5.71$ if you forget the 0.85 -- that is the trap. The 7.56 in. choice uses $b = 12$ instead of 14. The 4.00 in. choice is just $A_s$ -- a nonsensical substitution.

statement: In the ACI flexure formula $M_n = A_s f_y (d - a/2)$, the term $(d - a/2)$ represents the internal moment arm. Why is it measured from the centroid of tension steel to half the stress block depth rather than to the top of the beam?

choices.text: The resultant concrete compression force acts at the centroid of the Whitney stress block, which is at $a/2$ from the top
The concrete is assumed to carry no tension, so only the top half matters
The stress block depth $a$ always equals $d$, making the arm $d/2$
ACI uses $d - a/2$ as a safety reduction, not an actual moment arm

explanation: The Whitney stress block replaces the actual nonlinear compression zone with a uniform rectangular block of depth $a$. The resultant compressive force $C = 0.85 f_c' b a$ acts at the centroid of this rectangle, which is $a/2$ from the compression face. The tension force $T = A_s f_y$ acts at the centroid of the steel, located at depth $d$. The moment is force times lever arm: $M_n = T \times (d - a/2)$. The "concrete carries no tension" choice is partially true but does not explain the lever arm formula. The choice claiming $a$ always equals $d$ is wrong — $a$ is much smaller than $d$ in typical designs. The choice calling $d - a/2$ a safety reduction is wrong — this is a real mechanics derivation, not an arbitrary reduction.

statement: A concrete beam has $V_u = 20 \text{ kips}$ at the critical section and $\phi V_c = 30 \text{ kips}$. What is the shear reinforcement requirement?

choices.text: Provide minimum stirrups — $\phi V_c/2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$
Enlarge the section — concrete cannot carry any shear at all

explanation: $\phi V_c/2 = 30/2 = 15$ kips. Since $\phi V_c/2 = 15 < V_u = 20 \leq \phi V_c = 30$, the code says provide minimum stirrups. The threshold is: $V_u \leq \phi V_c/2$ means no stirrups; $\phi V_c/2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$ means minimum stirrups; $V_u > \phi V_c$ means design stirrups for $V_s$. With $V_u = 20$ falling between $\phi V_c/2 = 15$ and $\phi V_c = 30$, minimum stirrups are required. The "no stirrups needed" choice would require $V_u \leq 15$. The "design stirrups for computed $V_s$" choice would require $V_u > 30$. The "enlarge the section" choice is wrong — concrete absolutely carries shear through $V_c$.

statement: The ACI column capacity formula includes a 0.80 factor for tied columns (0.85 for spiral columns). What does this factor account for?

choices.text: A material safety factor equivalent to the resistance factor $\phi$
The difference in concrete strength between cylinders and the actual column
The weight of the column itself, which reduces its load-carrying capacity
Accidental eccentricity — columns never truly carry pure concentric axial load

explanation: In practice, no column carries a perfectly centered axial load. Construction tolerances, member crookedness, and load eccentricities introduce bending even when the design intent is pure compression. The 0.80 factor (0.85 for spiral columns) reduces the theoretical capacity to account for this inevitable moment. Spiral columns get a slightly more favorable factor because spirals provide better confinement and ductility, allowing the column to maintain capacity under eccentric loading. The cylinder-vs-actual-strength choice describes the 0.85 $f_c'$ coefficient in the stress block, not the 0.80 column factor. The self-weight choice is wrong — self-weight is handled through loads, not capacity reduction. The choice equating it with $\phi$ confuses it with the resistance factor, which is a separate reliability factor.

statement: A concrete column has $\varepsilon_t = 0.0015$ (net tensile strain in the extreme tension steel). What is the section classification and the correct $\phi$ factor for a tied column?

choices.text: Cannot be determined without knowing $f_c'$ and $f_y$

explanation: ACI classifies sections by the net tensile strain $\varepsilon_t$ in the extreme tension reinforcement at nominal strength. If $\varepsilon_t \leq 0.002$, the section is compression-controlled -- the concrete crushes before the steel yields significantly. For tied columns, $\phi = 0.65$. If $\varepsilon_t \geq 0.005$, the section is tension-controlled with $\phi = 0.90$. Between 0.002 and 0.005 is the transition zone, where $\phi$ is interpolated. Here, $\varepsilon_t = 0.0015 < 0.002$, so the section is compression-controlled. The tension-controlled choice requires $\varepsilon_t \geq 0.005$. The transition-zone choice requires $\varepsilon_t$ between 0.002 and 0.005. The "cannot be determined" choice is wrong -- the classification depends only on strain, not material properties.

statement: A fully braced W-shape has $Z_x = 96 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. What is the LRFD design flexural strength $\phi_b M_n$?
explanation: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 96 = 4{,}800$ kip-in $= 400$ kip-ft. Then $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 400 = 360$ kip-ft. The 400 kip-ft choice is the nominal capacity without $\phi_b$. The 240 kip-ft choice is the ASD allowable: $M_p / \Omega_b = 400/1.67 = 240$. The 288 kip-ft choice comes from using $S_x$ instead of $Z_x$ (a typical $S_x/Z_x$ ratio of about 0.89 would give roughly this).

statement: A W-shape beam has full lateral bracing and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. The elastic section modulus is $S_x = 100 \text{ in}^3$ and the plastic section modulus is $Z_x = 112 \text{ in}^3$. Which modulus should be used for the LRFD plastic moment capacity?

choices.text: $Z_x = 112 \text{ in}^3$ — the plastic modulus is used for LRFD strength design
$S_x = 100 \text{ in}^3$ — the elastic modulus is always more conservative
Either one — they give the same design strength after applying $\phi$
$S_x$ for compact sections, $Z_x$ for non-compact sections

explanation: For LRFD, the plastic moment capacity is $M_p = F_y Z_x$, using the plastic section modulus. The plastic modulus accounts for the full cross-section reaching yield stress, which is the actual failure mode for compact sections with full bracing. $S_x$ (elastic modulus) is used in the lateral-torsional buckling formula as the lower-bound term ($0.7 F_y S_x$) and in ASD. Using $S_x$ for the plastic moment underestimates capacity by about 10–15% for typical W-shapes. The $S_x$ choice is more conservative but incorrect for LRFD — LRFD is calibrated to use $Z_x$. The choice that swaps moduli by compactness has it backwards.

statement: A W-shape has $d = 14 \text{ in.}$, $t_w = 0.415 \text{ in.}$, and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. With $C_{v1} = 1.0$ and $\phi_v = 1.00$, what is the LRFD design shear strength $\phi_v V_n$?
explanation: $A_w = d \times t_w = 14 \times 0.415 = 5.81$ in$^2$. $V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1} = 0.6(50)(5.81)(1.0) = 174.3 \approx 174$ kips. With $\phi_v = 1.00$: $\phi_v V_n = 174$ kips. The 291 kips option uses $F_y A_w = 50 \times 5.81 = 291$ without the $0.6$ factor. The 350 kips option uses the full section area instead of web area. The 145 kips option incorrectly uses $\phi_v = 0.90$ or applies $0.5 F_y$ instead of $0.6 F_y$.

statement: A W-shape beam has $M_p = 600 \text{ kip-ft}$, $L_p = 10 \text{ ft}$, and $L_r = 30 \text{ ft}$. The unbraced length is $L_b = 10 \text{ ft}$. A second identical beam has $L_b = 20 \text{ ft}$ with $C_b = 1.0$. How do their nominal flexural strengths compare?

choices.text: The second beam has elastic LTB since $L_b > L_r$
Both beams reach $M_p = 600$ because they use the same section
Both are reduced by LTB because neither is continuously braced
The first beam reaches $M_p = 600$; the second is reduced below $M_p$ by inelastic LTB

explanation: The first beam has $L_b = 10 = L_p$, so it is fully braced and reaches $M_n = M_p = 600$ kip-ft. The second beam has $L_p = 10 < L_b = 20 \leq L_r = 30$, so it falls in the inelastic LTB zone. Its capacity is reduced by the linear interpolation formula: $M_n = M_p - (M_p - 0.7 F_y S_x)(L_b - L_p)/(L_r - L_p) < M_p$. The "both reach $M_p$" choice ignores the effect of unbraced length — same section does not mean same capacity if bracing conditions differ. The "both are reduced by LTB" choice is wrong because the first beam meets $L_b \leq L_p$. The "elastic LTB" choice is wrong because $L_b = 20 < L_r = 30$, so the second beam is in inelastic LTB, not elastic.

statement: A steel column has pin-pin supports ($K = 1.0$), an unbraced length of $10 \text{ ft}$, and $r_y = 1.50 \text{ in.}$ What is the slenderness ratio $KL/r_y$?
explanation: Convert $KL$ to inches: $1.0 \times 10 \times 12 = 120$ in. Then $KL/r_y = 120/1.50 = 80$. The 120 distractor is $KL$ in inches without dividing by $r$. The 6.7 distractor forgets to convert feet to inches: $10/1.50 \approx 6.7$. The 40 distractor uses half the length or otherwise miscounts the unit conversion.

statement: A cantilever column has a recommended effective length factor $K = 2.10$. A pin-pin column has $K = 1.0$. If both have the same physical length and cross-section, which has the lower design compressive strength?

choices.text: Both have the same strength because they have the same cross-section
The pin-pin column — its lower $K$ means less restraint and lower capacity
The cantilever — its larger $K$ produces a higher $KL/r$, reducing $\phi_c F_{cr}$
The cantilever — but only because it has a different $\phi_c$ factor

explanation: The effective length factor $K$ converts the physical length into an equivalent pin-pin length for buckling. A cantilever ($K = 2.10$) has an effective length more than twice the physical length because one end is free to translate. This dramatically increases $KL/r$, which reduces the critical buckling stress $F_{cr}$. The pin-pin column ($K = 1.0$) buckles over exactly its physical length. Higher $KL/r$ always means lower strength. The choice claiming the pin-pin column is weaker confuses $K$ with restraint — lower $K$ actually means MORE restraint (better support conditions). The choice saying both have the same strength ignores the role of end conditions. The choice blaming a different $\phi_c$ factor is wrong because $\phi_c = 0.90$ for both.

statement: A W-shape column has $r_x = 6.0 \text{ in.}$ and $r_y = 2.0 \text{ in.}$ The column is braced at every $12 \text{ ft}$ in the strong axis and at every $6 \text{ ft}$ in the weak axis (both pin-pin, $K = 1.0$). Which axis controls buckling?

choices.text: Neither controls — check only the axis with the larger $r$ value
Strong axis controls because it has the longer unbraced length
Weak axis controls because $r_y < r_x$, regardless of bracing
Strong axis ($KL/r_x = 24$) and weak axis ($KL/r_y = 36$) — weak axis controls with the larger ratio

explanation: Strong axis: $KL/r_x = (1.0 \times 12 \times 12)/6.0 = 144/6.0 = 24$. Weak axis: $KL/r_y = (1.0 \times 6 \times 12)/2.0 = 72/2.0 = 36$. The weak axis has the larger slenderness ratio ($36 > 24$), so it controls. Even though the weak axis has a shorter unbraced length (6 ft vs. 12 ft), $r_y$ is so much smaller than $r_x$ that it still produces the larger $KL/r$. The "strong axis controls because it has the longer unbraced length" choice only considers length, not the radius of gyration. The "weak axis controls because $r_y < r_x$, regardless of bracing" choice states the conclusion correctly but for the wrong reason — you must compute both ratios, not assume. The "check only the axis with the larger $r$ value" choice is backwards — check the axis with the LARGER $KL/r$, not the larger $r$.

statement: A flat bar ($3/8 \text{ in.} \times 8 \text{ in.}$) has two $3/4 \text{-in.}$ diameter bolts at the same cross-section. What is the net area $A_n$?
explanation: Each bolt hole subtracts $d_b + 1/8\text{"} = 3/4 + 1/8 = 7/8 = 0.875$ in. from the gross width. With two holes: net width $= 8 - 2(0.875) = 8 - 1.75 = 6.25$ in. Then $A_n = 6.25 \times 3/8 = 6.25 \times 0.375 = 2.34$ in$^2$. The 2.44 choice subtracts only $d_b = 0.75$ per hole without the 1/8" addition: $(8 - 1.50)(0.375) = 2.44$. The 3.00 choice is the gross area with no deductions. The 2.63 choice subtracts only one hole instead of two.

statement: Why does AISC use a lower resistance factor ($\phi = 0.75$) for tensile rupture than for tensile yielding ($\phi = 0.90$)?

choices.text: Rupture is a sudden, brittle failure with no warning, so a larger safety margin is needed
Rupture uses a higher material strength ($F_u$), so the factor must compensate
Rupture only occurs in low-grade steels that need extra conservatism
The lower factor accounts for bolt hole drilling inaccuracy

explanation: Yielding spreads across the gross section gradually — the member elongates and gives visible warning before failure. Rupture, on the other hand, happens suddenly at the weakest net section with little plastic deformation. Because rupture is a more dangerous failure mode (no warning, no redistribution), AISC applies a lower resistance factor to build in a larger safety margin. The "higher material strength (Fu)" choice confuses material strength with reliability philosophy. The "low-grade steels only" choice is wrong — rupture can occur in any grade of steel. The "bolt hole drilling inaccuracy" choice is partially related (hole deductions matter) but the fundamental reason is the brittle failure mode.

statement: An angle connected by bolts through only one leg is used as a tension brace. Compared to a flat bar connected through its full width (both with the same $A_n$), how does the angle's effective net area $A_e$ differ?

choices.text: $A_e$ is the same — $U = 1.0$ for all tension members
$A_e$ is larger because the unconnected leg adds extra capacity
$A_e$ is smaller because the shear lag factor $U < 1.0$ reduces the effective area for the unconnected leg
$A_e$ is smaller because angles use a different $\phi$ factor

explanation: When a tension member is connected through only part of its cross-section (like an angle bolted through one leg), the stress does not distribute uniformly across the full section. The unconnected leg experiences "shear lag" — it cannot fully develop its tensile capacity before the connection ends. AISC accounts for this with the shear lag factor $U = 1 - \bar{x}/L$, where $\bar{x}$ is the distance from the connection plane to the centroid of the member and $L$ is the connection length. For a flat bar bolted through its full width, all elements are connected so $U = 1.0$. For an angle connected through one leg, $U < 1.0$, reducing $A_e = U \cdot A_n$. The "larger because the unconnected leg adds extra capacity" option is backwards. The "same, U = 1.0 for all tension members" option is only true for fully connected members. The "different phi factor" option confuses shear lag with resistance factors.

statement: At a truss joint, an $8\text{ kN}$ vertical (downward) load is resisted by a horizontal member and a diagonal member inclined at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is the force in the diagonal?
explanation: Only the diagonal resists the vertical load. $\sum F_y = 0$: $F\sin 60^\circ = 8$, so $F = 8/0.866 = 9.24\text{ kN}$. The 6.93 kN option multiplies by sin 60° instead of dividing. The 8.0 kN option forgets the angle entirely.

statement: A vertical section through a parallel-chord truss cuts a diagonal inclined at $45^\circ$. The net vertical shear carried across that section is $20\text{ kN}$. What is the force in the diagonal?
explanation: Only the diagonal has a vertical component, so it carries the section shear: $F\sin 45^\circ = 20$, giving $F = 20/0.707 = 28.3\text{ kN}$. The 14.1 kN option multiplies by sin 45° instead of dividing.

statement: A beam is fixed (built in) at both ends with no internal hinges. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
explanation: Each fixed end gives 3 reactions (H, V, M), so $r = 6$. A planar beam has 3 equilibrium equations, so $DSI = 6 - 3 = 3$. The choice giving 1 is a propped cantilever, not fixed-fixed. The choice giving 6 forgets to subtract the equilibrium equations.

statement: A rigid plane frame has $m = 6$ members and $j = 6$ joints. Both bases are fixed supports and there are no internal hinges ($c = 0$). What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
explanation: For a plane frame, compare $3m + r$ to $3j + c$. Two fixed supports give $r = 3 + 3 = 6$ reaction components. Then $3m + r = 3(6) + 6 = 24$, and $3j + c = 3(6) + 0 = 18$. The degree of indeterminacy is $24 - 18 = 6$. The value 3 results from counting only one fixed support ($r = 3$): $21 - 18 = 3$. The value 4 results from treating each base as a pin ($r = 4$): $22 - 18 = 4$. The value 0 wrongly applies the truss formula $m + r$ vs $2j$.

statement: A single straight beam (one rigid member) is supported by a pin at one end and a pin at the other end, with no internal hinges. Treating it as a planar beam with 3 equilibrium equations, how is it classified externally?

choices.text: Stable and externally indeterminate to the 1st degree
Stable and externally indeterminate to the 3rd degree

explanation: Each pin provides 2 reaction components, so $r = 2 + 2 = 4$. A planar beam has 3 independent equilibrium equations ($\Sigma F_x = 0$, $\Sigma F_y = 0$, $\Sigma M = 0$). The external degree of indeterminacy is $r - 3 = 4 - 3 = 1$. Two pins introduce one redundant horizontal restraint that equilibrium alone cannot resolve. The "stable and statically determinate" choice would require exactly $r = 3$, which is the familiar pin-plus-roller case. The "unstable — mechanism" choice would require $r < 3$. The "indeterminate to the 3rd degree" choice overcounts the redundancy — only one extra reaction component exists beyond the three equilibrium equations.

statement: A beam carries $D = 40 \text{ kips}$, floor live load $L = 30 \text{ kips}$, and snow $S = 24 \text{ kips}$. Using the ASD combination $D + 0.75L + 0.75(L_r \text{ or } S \text{ or } R)$, what is the design (service-level) load?
explanation: ASD uses unfactored loads with the 0.75 companion factor: $D + 0.75L + 0.75S = 40 + 0.75(30) + 0.75(24) = 40 + 22.5 + 18 = 80.5$ kips. The 94 kips option is the plain sum $D + L + S = 40 + 30 + 24$, forgetting the 0.75 factors. The 84 kips option is the LRFD combination $1.2D + 1.6L = 48 + 48$ — wrong because the problem specifies ASD. The 62.5 kips option drops the snow term and uses only $D + 0.75L = 40 + 22.5$.

statement: A heavily loaded transfer girder supports $D = 100 \text{ kips}$ and a small floor live load $L = 10 \text{ kips}$ (no snow, wind, or seismic). Which LRFD combination controls and what is the controlling factored load?
explanation: Combination 1 is $1.4D = 1.4(100) = 140$ kips. Combination 2 is $1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(100) + 1.6(10) = 120 + 16 = 136$ kips. Because dead load dominates and live load is small, Combination 1 (140) produces the larger factored load and controls. This is the case the $1.4D$ combination exists for. The 136 kips option is Combination 2, which is smaller here. The 120 kips option keeps only the $1.2D$ term and drops live load. The 110 kips option is the unfactored service load $D + L$.

statement: A simply supported beam carries a uniform load over its entire span. Using the influence line for shear at midspan (which is positive to the right of the cut and negative to the left, with equal triangular areas), what is the shear at midspan?

choices.text: Zero — the equal positive and negative IL areas cancel
Equal to the midspan moment divided by $L$

explanation: The IL for shear at midspan is antisymmetric: a positive triangle on the right half and an equal negative triangle on the left half. For a uniform load over the whole span, the shear equals $w$ times the net area under the IL. Because the positive and negative areas are equal in magnitude, they cancel and the net shear at midspan is zero. This matches the familiar result that shear is zero at the point of maximum moment in a symmetric beam. The "maximum positive" and "maximum negative" choices assume the load sits on only one half of the span. The choice equating shear to the midspan moment divided by L confuses the shear-moment relationship.

statement: A reinforced concrete beam ($d = 22 \text{ in.}$) uses #4 U-stirrups ($A_v = 0.40 \text{ in}^2$ for two legs) with $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$ spaced at $s = 8 \text{ in.}$ What is the shear strength contributed by the stirrups, $V_s$?
explanation: $V_s = \frac{A_v f_y d}{s} = \frac{0.40 \times 60 \times 22}{8} = \frac{528}{8} = 66$ kips. The 33 kips option uses only one stirrup leg ($A_v = 0.20$) instead of the two-leg area. The 132 kips option halves the spacing to $s = 4$ in. by mistake. The 30 kips option drops $d$ and uses an incorrect lever term.

statement: A designer proposes a tied column with a longitudinal reinforcement ratio of $\rho_g = 0.10$ (10 percent). Per ACI 318, what is the issue?

choices.text: It is acceptable — there is no upper limit on $\rho_g$
It is below the 1 percent minimum, risking brittle failure
It exceeds the 8 percent maximum, causing bar congestion and poor concrete placement
It is only a problem for spiral columns, not tied columns

explanation: ACI limits the longitudinal steel ratio to $0.01 \leq \rho_g \leq 0.08$ (1 to 8 percent). A 10 percent ratio exceeds the 8 percent maximum. The upper limit prevents reinforcement congestion that makes it impossible to place and consolidate concrete around the bars and at lap splices. The "acceptable — no upper limit" choice is wrong because an upper limit exists. The "below the 1 percent minimum" choice has the direction backwards — 10 percent is far above, not below, the minimum. The "only a problem for spiral columns" choice is wrong because the limits apply to both tied and spiral columns.

statement: A fully braced W-shape has $Z_x = 100 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. What is the ASD allowable flexural strength $M_n/\Omega_b$?
explanation: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 100 = 5{,}000$ kip-in $= 416.7$ kip-ft. For ASD, divide by $\Omega_b = 1.67$: $M_n/\Omega_b = 416.7/1.67 = 249.5 \approx 250$ kip-ft. The 417 kip-ft choice is the nominal $M_n$ without applying $\Omega_b$. The 375 kip-ft choice is the LRFD design strength $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 416.7$ — the problem asks for ASD. The 278 kip-ft choice uses an incorrect $\Omega_b = 1.50$.

statement: A W-shape has $d = 18 \text{ in.}$, $t_w = 0.30 \text{ in.}$, and $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$. With $C_{v1} = 1.0$ and $\phi_v = 1.00$, what is the LRFD design shear strength $\phi_v V_n$?
explanation: Web area $A_w = d \times t_w = 18 \times 0.30 = 5.40$ in$^2$. Nominal shear $V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1} = 0.6(36)(5.40)(1.0) = 116.6$ kips. With $\phi_v = 1.00$: $\phi_v V_n = 117$ kips. The 194 kips choice omits the 0.6 coefficient ($36 \times 5.40 = 194$). The 162 kips choice uses $0.5 F_y$ instead of $0.6 F_y$ on a larger web area. The 105 kips choice applies $\phi_v = 0.90$ instead of $1.00$ ($0.9 \times 116.6 = 105$).

statement: A steel column has $KL/r = 90$, $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$, and $E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$. Which buckling regime governs, and how do you know?

choices.text: Elastic buckling, because $KL/r > 50$ always means elastic
Cannot be determined without the cross-sectional area

explanation: The dividing line between inelastic and elastic column buckling is $4.71\sqrt{E/F_y} = 4.71\sqrt{29{,}000/50} = 4.71\sqrt{580} = 4.71(24.08) = 113.4$. Since the column slenderness $KL/r = 90$ is less than 113.4, the column buckles inelastically and uses $F_{cr} = 0.658^{F_y/F_e} F_y$. The "elastic buckling, because $KL/r = 90 > 113$" choice has the inequality backwards. The "$KL/r > 50$ always means elastic" choice uses an arbitrary cutoff of 50, which is not the AISC threshold. The "cannot be determined without the cross-sectional area" choice is wrong — the regime depends only on $KL/r$, $E$, and $F_y$, not on area.

statement: A single angle is bolted through one leg as a tension member. Its net area is $A_n = 4.00 \text{ in}^2$, the distance from the connection plane to the member centroid is $\bar{x} = 1.20 \text{ in.}$, and the connection length is $L = 9.0 \text{ in.}$ What is the effective net area $A_e$?
explanation: The shear lag factor is $U = 1 - \bar{x}/L = 1 - 1.20/9.0 = 1 - 0.1333 = 0.867$. The effective net area is $A_e = U A_n = 0.867 \times 4.00 = 3.47$ in$^2$. The 4.00 in$^2$ choice assumes $U = 1.0$, which only applies when all cross-sectional elements are connected. The 0.87 in$^2$ choice reports $U$ itself, not $A_e$. The 3.20 in$^2$ choice subtracts $\bar{x} \times A_n / L$ incorrectly or uses $U = 0.80$.

statement: A beam fixed at both ends spans $L = 6\text{ m}$ and carries a central point load $P = 24\text{ kN}$. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support?
explanation: Fixed-fixed beam, central point load: the fixed-end moment is $PL/8 = 24(6)/8 = 18\text{ kN·m}$. The 36 kN·m choice uses $PL/4$ (the simple-span midspan moment). The 144 kN·m choice forgets to divide entirely.

statement: A fully saturated soil has a water content $\omega = 20\%$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$. What is the void ratio $e$?
explanation: When soil is fully saturated, S = 1. The master relationship Se = wGs becomes e = wGs = 0.20 × 2.70 = 0.54. The 0.74 choice might come from using w = 0.274 or a different Gs. The 2.70 choice is just the specific gravity. The 0.20 choice confuses the water content with the void ratio.

statement: A soil has 80% passing the No. 200 sieve, $LL = 45$, and $PI = 22$. What is its USCS classification?
explanation: More than 50% passes #200, so it is fine-grained. LL = 45 < 50, so it is low-plasticity (L). On the A-line at LL = 45: PI = 0.73(45 – 20) = 18.25. Since the actual PI = 22 > 18.25, the soil plots above the A-line → clay (C). Combine: CL (lean clay). ML would be below the A-line. CH requires LL ≥ 50. SC is a coarse-grained soil with clay fines.

statement: A sand has $D_{10} = 0.15 \text{ mm}$, $D_{30} = 0.50 \text{ mm}$, $D_{60} = 2.0 \text{ mm}$. Less than 5% passes the No. 200 sieve. What is its USCS classification?
explanation: Less than 50% passes #200 → coarse. It is identified as a sand (more than 50% of the coarse fraction passes the No. 4 sieve). With < 5% fines, classify based on gradation. Cu = D60/D10 = 2.0/0.15 = 13.3 (need ≥ 6 ✔). Cc = (D30)²/(D10 × D60) = 0.25/0.30 = 0.83 (need 1–3 ✘). Since Cc fails the range, it is poorly graded: SP. The SW option requires BOTH the Cu and Cc criteria to be met. The SM option would need > 12% fines.

statement: A soil has $LL = 55$, $PI = 28$, and 60% passing the No. 200 sieve. What is the USCS classification?
explanation: 60% passes #200 → fine-grained. LL = 55 > 50 → high plasticity (H). A-line at LL = 55: PI = 0.73(55 – 20) = 25.6. Actual PI = 28 > 25.6 → above A-line → clay (C). Classification: CH (fat clay). The MH choice is below the A-line (silt). The CL choice requires LL < 50. The OH choice is an organic soil which requires lab testing (oven-dried LL) — not determinable from the given data alone, so assume inorganic.

statement: A 10-ft-thick saturated soil layer has $\gamma_{sat} = 115 \text{ pcf}$. The water table is at the ground surface. What is the effective stress at the bottom of the layer?
explanation: σ = γsat × H = 115 × 10 = 1,150 psf. u = γw × H = 62.4 × 10 = 624 psf. σ' = 1,150 – 624 = 526 psf. Or use the shortcut: σ' = γ' × H = (115 – 62.4) × 10 = 52.6 × 10 = 526 psf. The 1,150 psf option is the total stress — forgetting to subtract pore pressure. The 624 psf option is the pore pressure itself.

statement: A site has 5 ft of dry sand ($\gamma = 110 \text{ pcf}$) over 8 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 120 \text{ pcf}$). The water table is at the sand-clay interface. What is the effective vertical stress at the bottom of the clay?
explanation: Total stress at the bottom: σ = 110(5) + 120(8) = 550 + 960 = 1,510 psf. Pore pressure: u = 62.4(8) = 499 psf (water is 8 ft deep below the WT). Effective: σ' = 1,510 – 499 = 1,011 psf. The 1,510 psf option is the total stress. The 960 psf option is only the clay layer contribution without the sand above. The 526 psf option uses only the buoyant weight of clay without the sand overburden.

statement: A site has a $100 \text{ psf}$ uniform surcharge on the surface. Below: 6 ft of sand ($\gamma = 105 \text{ pcf}$, above WT) over 10 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 118 \text{ pcf}$). The WT is at the sand-clay interface. What is the effective vertical stress at the bottom of the clay?
explanation: Total stress: σ = 100 + 105(6) + 118(10) = 100 + 630 + 1,180 = 1,910 psf. Pore pressure: u = 62.4(10) = 624 psf. Effective: σ' = 1,910 – 624 = 1,286 psf. The surcharge adds to total stress but NOT to pore pressure. The 1,910 psf option forgets to subtract u. The 1,186 psf option forgot the surcharge. The 1,810 psf option subtracted the surcharge from total stress instead of subtracting pore pressure.

statement: For the clay in Problem 1, $c_v = 0.50 \text{ ft}^2\text{/day}$ with two-way drainage ($H_{dr} = 5 \text{ ft}$). How long does it take for 50% consolidation? Use $T_v = 0.197$ at $U = 50\%$.
explanation: Tv = cv·t/Hdr² → t = Tv·Hdr²/cv = 0.197 × 25/0.50 = 9.85 ≈ 10 days. Two-way drainage means Hdr = H/2 = 5 ft. The 20 days choice uses Hdr = 10 ft (one-way drainage). The 5 days choice might divide by 2 again. The 39 days choice uses Tv = 0.785 (for U = 90%).

statement: A soil has $c' = 200 \text{ psf}$ and $\phi' = 30\degree$. What is the shear strength on a plane where the effective normal stress is $\sigma_N' = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$?
explanation: τf = c’ + σN’ tan φ’ = 200 + 1,000 × tan 30° = 200 + 1,000 × 0.5774 = 200 + 577 = 777 psf. The 577 psf option forgot the cohesion term. The 1,000 psf option is just the normal stress. The 200 psf option is just the cohesion — ignoring the frictional component entirely.

statement: A triaxial test on a cohesionless soil ($c = 0$) gives $\sigma_1 = 6{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and $\sigma_3 = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the friction angle $\phi$?
explanation: For c = 0: sin φ = (σ1 – σ3)/(σ1 + σ3) = (6,000 – 2,000)/(6,000 + 2,000) = 4,000/8,000 = 0.50. φ = arcsin(0.50) = 30°. The 45° choice might come from using tan⁻¹(σ1/σ3) incorrectly. The 26.6° choice is arctan(0.50) — a common mistake from using tan instead of sin.

statement: An unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial test on a saturated clay gives $\sigma_3 = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$ and $(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) = 2{,}400 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the undrained cohesion $c_u$?
explanation: In a UU test on saturated clay, φu = 0. The Mohr circle has its center at s = (σ1+σ3)/2 and radius t = (σ1–σ3)/2. For φ = 0, the failure envelope is a horizontal line at τ = cu, and cu = the radius = (σ1–σ3)/2 = 2,400/2 = 1,200 psf. The 2,400 psf choice is the deviator stress itself, not halved. The 2,700 psf choice is (σ1+σ3)/2 = (3,900+1,500)/2 — that is the center of the Mohr circle, not the radius. The 1,500 psf choice is just σ3.

statement: Water flows through a soil sample with hydraulic conductivity $k = 0.01\text{ cm/s}$ under a hydraulic gradient $i = 0.5$. The cross-sectional area is $A = 100\text{ cm}^2$. What is the flow rate?
explanation: Darcy: q = kiA = 0.01 × 0.5 × 100 = 0.5 cm³/s. The 5.0 cm^3/s option inflates the result tenfold. The 0.05 cm^3/s option multiplies in an extra factor of 0.1. The 50 cm^3/s option drops the gradient and shifts a decimal.

statement: A saturated sand has specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$ and void ratio $e = 0.85$. What is the critical hydraulic gradient at which a quick condition occurs?
explanation: i_c = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e) = (2.70 − 1)/(1 + 0.85) = 1.70/1.85 = 0.92. The 1.00 choice wrongly assumes i_c is always exactly 1.0. The 1.85 choice just reports the denominator (1 + e) = 1.85 instead of the full ratio. The 0.54 choice inverts the fraction, using (1 + e)/(Gs − 1) instead of (Gs − 1)/(1 + e).

statement: Seepage beneath a dam is analyzed with a flow net having $N_f = 4$ flow channels and $N_d = 12$ equipotential drops. The hydraulic conductivity is $k = 2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$ and the total head loss is $H = 6\text{ m}$. What is the seepage rate per unit width?
explanation: q = kH(Nf/Nd) = (2×10⁻⁵)(6)(4/12) = (2×10⁻⁵)(6)(0.333) = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m³/s per m. The 3.6×10⁻⁴ choice inverts the ratio (Nd/Nf = 12/4 = 3). The 1.0×10⁻⁵ choice mishandles the head. The 2.4×10⁻⁴ choice uses an incorrect ratio value.

statement: A dry cohesionless sand slope is inclined at $\beta = 20\degree$. The soil's friction angle is $\phi = 34\degree$. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
explanation: For a dry cohesionless infinite slope, FS = tan φ / tan β = tan 34° / tan 20° = 0.6745/0.3640 = 1.85. The 0.54 choice inverts the ratio (tan β / tan φ). The 1.70 choice subtracts angles incorrectly. The 0.93 choice applies a seepage reduction that is not present here.

statement: The same cohesionless slope ($\phi = 34\degree$, $\beta = 20\degree$) becomes fully saturated with seepage parallel to the slope. With $\gamma_{sat} = 19.62\text{ kN/m}^3$ and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, what is the new factor of safety?
explanation: With seepage, FS = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β). Here γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = 19.62 − 9.81 = 9.81, so γ′/γ_sat = 9.81/19.62 = 0.5. The dry FS was 1.85, so FS = 0.5 × 1.85 = 0.93 — now UNSTABLE. The 1.85 option ignores seepage (it is the dry FS). The 3.70 option multiplies by tan φ/tan β twice instead of reducing. The 0.50 option reports only the reduction factor.

statement: A strip footing rests on clay with undrained shear strength $c_u = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$. Using $\phi = 0$ factors ($N_c = 5.14$, $N_q = 1$, $N_\gamma = 0$) and footing depth $D_f = 0$, what is the ultimate bearing capacity?
explanation: qult = cNc + γ’(0)Nq + 0 = 1,500 × 5.14 + 0 + 0 = 7,710 psf. With Df = 0, the overburden term vanishes. The 1,500 psf option is just the cohesion. The 5,140 psf option uses c = 1,000 or confuses Nc with the answer. The 3,855 psf option divides by FS = 2 prematurely — the problem asks for ultimate, not allowable.

statement: A soil has $\phi' = 30\degree$. What is the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient $K_a$?
explanation: Ka = tan²(45° – 30°/2) = tan²(30°) = (0.5774)² = 0.333 = 1/3. The 3.0 option is Kp, the passive coefficient (or 1/Ka). The 0.577 option is tan 30°, not tan² 30°. The 0.50 option is sin 30°.

statement: A 15-ft-tall retaining wall has backfill with $\phi' = 30\degree$, $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, $c = 0$. What is the total active force per foot of wall?
explanation: Ka = 1/3 (from φ = 30°). Pa = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H² = 0.5 × (1/3) × 120 × 15² = 0.5 × 0.333 × 120 × 225 = 4,500 lb/ft. The 9,000 lb/ft choice forgets the 1/2 factor (uses KaγH² instead of 0.5KaγH²). The 13,500 lb/ft choice omits Ka entirely (uses Ka = 1: 0.5 x 1 x 120 x 225 = 13,500). The 2,250 lb/ft choice divides by 2 an extra time.

statement: A retaining wall has total resisting moment $\Sigma M_R = 15{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$ and overturning moment $M_O = 5{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$ about the toe. What is the factor of safety against overturning?
explanation: FS = ΣMR / MO = 15,000/5,000 = 3.0. This is a direct formula application. The 2.0 option might come from dividing something else. The 5.0 option reversed a number. The 0.33 option inverted the ratio (MO/MR).

statement: A retaining wall has total vertical force $\Sigma V = 5{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$, base width $B = 6 \text{ ft}$, $\Sigma M_R = 18{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$, and $M_O = 6{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$. What is the eccentricity $e$ of the resultant on the base?
explanation: First find where the resultant hits the base (measured from the toe): x̄ = (ΣMR – MO)/ΣV = (18,000 – 6,000)/5,000 = 12,000/5,000 = 2.40 ft. Eccentricity from the center: e = B/2 – x̄ = 3.0 – 2.4 = 0.60 ft. Check: B/6 = 1.0 ft, and e = 0.60 < 1.0, so the resultant is in the middle third ✔. The 2.40 ft option is x̄, the distance from the toe, not the eccentricity from the center. The 3.00 ft option is B/2. The 1.20 ft option doubles e by mistake.

statement: A gravity retaining wall has base width $B = 8 \text{ ft}$. The resultant vertical force $\Sigma V = 8{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$ acts $3.0 \text{ ft}$ from the toe. What is the maximum pressure at the toe?
explanation: Eccentricity: e = B/2 – x̄ = 4.0 – 3.0 = 1.0 ft. Check: B/6 = 8/6 = 1.33 ft, and e = 1.0 < 1.33 ✔ (in middle third). Toe pressure: qtoe = (ΣV/B)(1 + 6e/B) = (8,000/8)(1 + 6(1.0)/8) = 1,000(1 + 0.75) = 1,000 × 1.75 = 1,750 psf. The 1,000 psf option is the uniform pressure (ΣV/B) without the eccentricity effect. The 2,000 psf option uses e = B/6 = 1.33. The 1,333 psf option might come from a different eccentricity.

statement: A pile has a unit end-bearing resistance $q_p = 2{,}000\text{ kPa}$ over a tip area $A_p = 0.20\text{ m}^2$, and a unit skin friction $f_s = 50\text{ kPa}$ over a shaft surface area $A_s = 12\text{ m}^2$. What is the ultimate pile capacity?
explanation: Q_ult = Qp + Qs = qp·Ap + fs·As = (2,000)(0.20) + (50)(12) = 400 + 600 = 1,000 kN. The 400 kN option is only the end bearing. The 600 kN option is only the skin friction. The 2,600 kN option mistakenly uses the tip area as 1.0 m² (2,000 + 600).

statement: A site has 8 m of soft compressible clay overlying dense gravel. Why would a deep foundation be preferred over a shallow footing for a heavily loaded column?

choices.text: To transfer the load through the weak clay to the firm gravel, limiting settlement
Because deep foundations are always cheaper than footings
To increase the bearing pressure on the soft clay
Because shallow footings cannot be used under any column

explanation: The soft clay would settle excessively under a shallow footing. A deep foundation bypasses the weak clay and transfers the load to the dense gravel below, controlling settlement and providing adequate capacity. The claim that deep foundations are always cheaper is false (piles are usually more expensive). The option about increasing bearing pressure on the soft clay is backwards — you want to relieve, not increase, load on the clay. The claim that shallow footings can never be used overstates the case.

statement: Fill is placed over a soft clay layer through which a pile passes. As the clay consolidates and settles relative to the pile, what force develops on the pile shaft?

choices.text: Negative skin friction (downdrag), which adds load to the pile
Positive skin friction that increases the pile capacity
An upward buoyant force that relieves the pile
No force, because the clay and pile move together

explanation: When surrounding soil settles MORE than the pile, it drags down on the shaft — negative skin friction (downdrag). This acts as an additional downward load the pile must carry, not as support. The "positive skin friction increases capacity" choice reverses the direction. The "upward buoyant force" choice invents a relief that does not exist here. The "no force, clay and pile move together" choice ignores the relative settlement that causes downdrag.

statement: A field dry unit weight of $118\text{ pcf}$ is measured on a fill whose laboratory maximum dry unit weight (modified Proctor) is $124\text{ pcf}$. What is the relative compaction?
explanation: RC = (γd,field/γd,max) × 100 = (118/124) × 100 = 95.2%, which would satisfy a typical 95% specification. The 105% choice inverts the ratio (124/118). The 5.1% choice computes the percent difference (6/118). The 90.0% choice is a guess at the spec value.

statement: A sand has maximum void ratio $e_{max} = 0.90$, minimum void ratio $e_{min} = 0.40$, and an in-place void ratio $e = 0.60$. What is its relative density?
explanation: Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100 = (0.90 − 0.60)/(0.90 − 0.40) × 100 = 0.30/0.50 × 100 = 60% — a medium-dense sand. The 40% choice uses (e − emin) in the numerator. The 67% choice uses (e − emin)/(emax − e). The 33% choice inverts the numerator difference.

statement: A high-plasticity clay subgrade is too soft and swells when wet. Which chemical stabilizer is most appropriate?

choices.text: Portland cement (alone, in the plastic clay)
Fly ash used purely as a filler

explanation: Lime is the classic stabilizer for high-plasticity clays: it reduces the plasticity index, controls swelling, and improves workability and strength.
