Cement is more effective in granular and low-plasticity soils. Adding water would worsen a swelling clay, and fly ash as a mere filler does not chemically stabilize it.

statement: A soil sample has a void ratio $e = 0.65$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$. What is the porosity $n$?
explanation: Porosity relates to void ratio by $n = e/(1+e) = 0.65/(1+0.65) = 0.65/1.65 = 0.394$. The 0.650 option is the void ratio itself, not the porosity. The 0.241 option might come from $e/(1+G_s)$. The 0.606 option might come from $1/(1+e)$, which is the reciprocal relationship.

statement: A soil sample is tested and found to have a degree of saturation $S = 100\%$. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: The soil contains no air and no water
All void space is filled with water, and $e = \omega G_s$

explanation: When $S = 100\%$, the voids are completely filled with water (no air phase). The master relationship $Se = \omega G_s$ simplifies to $e = \omega G_s$. The "no air and no water" choice is backwards -- full saturation means all voids have water, not that the soil is completely dry. The "void ratio must equal 1.0" choice is wrong because $e$ depends on the soil structure, not saturation alone. The "water content equals $G_s$" choice mixes up the formula -- $\omega = e/G_s$ at full saturation, not $\omega = G_s$.

statement: A soil has total unit weight $\gamma = 125 \text{ pcf}$ and water content $\omega = 22\%$. What is the dry unit weight $\gamma_d$?
explanation: Dry unit weight strips out the water: $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega) = 125/(1+0.22) = 125/1.22 = 102.5$ pcf. The 97.5 pcf option might come from subtracting $\gamma \times \omega = 125 \times 0.22 = 27.5$, giving $125 - 27.5 = 97.5$ -- that is wrong because the water content is based on the weight of solids, not total weight. The 125 pcf option is the total unit weight, not dry. The 27.5 pcf option is just $\gamma \times \omega$, which has no physical meaning here.

statement: A contractor measures the water content $\omega$ and total unit weight $\gamma$ of a compacted fill. Which sequence correctly determines the degree of saturation?

choices.text: Compute $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega)$, then find $e$ from $\gamma_d = G_s \gamma_w/(1+e)$, then $S = \omega G_s / e$

explanation: To get $S$ you need $e$, and to get $e$ you need $\gamma_d$. Step 1: $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega)$ strips out the water weight. Step 2: rearranging $\gamma_d = G_s \gamma_w/(1+e)$ gives $e$. Step 3: $Se = \omega G_s$ gives $S = \omega G_s/e$. The $e = \omega G_s$ choice is wrong because $e = \omega G_s$ only works at full saturation ($S = 1$), and then computing $S = e/(1+e)$ is not the degree of saturation. The $\gamma_d = \gamma \times \omega$ choice makes up a formula -- $\gamma_d$ is not $\gamma \times \omega$. The $n = \omega/G_s$ choice also fabricates a relationship.

statement: A sand has $D_{10} = 0.25 \text{ mm}$, $D_{30} = 1.5 \text{ mm}$, and $D_{60} = 10 \text{ mm}$ with less than 5% fines. What is the coefficient of uniformity $C_u$?
explanation: $C_u = D_{60}/D_{10} = 10/0.25 = 40$. This is a direct formula plug-in. The value 6 is the minimum $C_u$ threshold for well-graded sand, not the calculated value. The value 0.90 is the coefficient of curvature $C_c = (D_{30})^2/(D_{10} \times D_{60})$. The value 4 is the minimum $C_u$ for well-graded gravel.

statement: A soil has 70% passing the No. 200 sieve, $LL = 40$, and $PI = 12$. On the USCS plasticity chart, the A-line value at $LL = 40$ is $PI_A = 0.73(40-20) = 14.6$. Since $PI = 12 < 14.6$, the soil plots below the A-line. What is the USCS classification?
explanation: 70% passing #200 means fine-grained. $LL = 40 < 50$ means low plasticity (L). The problem already tells you the soil plots below the A-line, which means silt (M). So the classification is ML (low-plasticity silt). CL would be above the A-line. SM is a coarse-grained soil with silty fines. MH requires $LL \geq 50$.

statement: A coarse-grained soil has 40% retained on the No. 4 sieve, 55% passing the No. 4 sieve and retained on the No. 200 sieve, and 5% passing the No. 200 sieve. The gradation coefficients are $C_u = 8$ and $C_c = 2.1$. What is the USCS classification?
explanation: Only 5% passes #200, so the soil is coarse-grained. Of the coarse fraction (95%), 55% passes the No. 4 sieve -- that is more than half, so it is a sand (S), not gravel (G). With < 5% fines, classify by gradation. For sand: $C_u \geq 6$ ($8 \geq 6$, passes) AND $1 \leq C_c \leq 3$ (2.1 is in range, passes). Both criteria met, so it is well-graded sand: SW. The GW option would require more than half the coarse fraction retained on the No. 4 sieve. The SP option would have one of the gradation criteria fail. The SM option requires > 12% fines.

statement: A fine-grained soil has $LL = 62$ and $PL = 25$. Compute the plasticity index and determine whether the soil plots above or below the A-line. What is the USCS classification?
explanation: $PI = LL - PL = 62 - 25 = 37$. The soil is fine-grained with $LL = 62 > 50$, so it is high plasticity (H). A-line at $LL = 62$: $PI_A = 0.73(62 - 20) = 0.73(42) = 30.7$. Actual $PI = 37 > 30.7$, so it plots above the A-line -- clay (C). Classification: CH (fat clay). MH would be below the A-line. CL requires $LL < 50$. OH is organic soil, which requires comparing oven-dried LL to natural LL -- not determinable from this data alone.

statement: A uniform surcharge $q$ is placed on the ground surface above a saturated clay layer. Which statement correctly describes the effect on effective stress at a point within the clay?

choices.text: Effective stress increases by $2q$ because both total stress and pore pressure increase by $q$
Both total stress and pore pressure increase by $q$, so effective stress is unchanged
The surcharge has no effect below the water table
Total stress increases by $q$ at all depths, but pore pressure is unchanged, so effective stress increases by $q$

explanation: A surface surcharge adds $q$ to the total vertical stress at every depth. However, it does not change the hydrostatic pore water pressure ($u = \gamma_w \times h_w$ is unchanged). Since $\sigma' = \sigma - u$, the effective stress increases by $q$. The "unchanged effective stress" option describes an undrained loading response in the short term, but the question is about the static equilibrium condition. The "no effect below the water table" option is wrong because surcharge absolutely affects stress below the WT. The "increases by $2q$" option invents a $2q$ increase that has no basis.

statement: A 12-ft-thick saturated clay layer has $\gamma_{sat} = 118 \text{ pcf}$ with the water table at the ground surface. What is the effective vertical stress at a depth of 8 ft?
explanation: $\sigma = \gamma_{sat} \times h = 118 \times 8 = 944$ psf. $u = \gamma_w \times h = 62.4 \times 8 = 499.2$ psf. $\sigma' = 944 - 499 = 445$ psf. Or use the shortcut: $\sigma' = \gamma' \times h = (118 - 62.4) \times 8 = 55.6 \times 8 = 444.8 \approx 445$ psf. The 944 psf choice is the total stress. The 499 psf choice is the pore water pressure. The 1,416 psf choice would come from using the full 12 ft instead of 8 ft.

statement: At a site, the water table drops by 5 ft due to pumping. The soil above the new water table was previously saturated and is now moist with $\gamma_{moist} = 110 \text{ pcf}$. What happens to the effective stress at a point 20 ft below the original water table?

choices.text: Effective stress decreases because the water table dropped
Effective stress stays the same because sigma and u both decrease equally
Effective stress increases because pore pressure decreases more than total stress decreases
Effective stress is unaffected because the point is still below the water table

explanation: When the WT drops 5 ft, pore pressure at our point decreases by $\gamma_w \times 5 = 62.4 \times 5 = 312$ psf. Total stress changes because the 5-ft zone above went from saturated (~120 pcf) to moist (110 pcf), so total stress decreases by about $(120 - 110) \times 5 = 50$ psf. Since $\sigma' = \sigma - u$, and $u$ decreased by 312 while $\sigma$ decreased by only 50, the net change in effective stress is +262 psf -- it increases. The "stays the same" choice is wrong because $\sigma$ and $u$ do not decrease equally. The "effective stress decreases" choice confuses direction. The "unaffected because still below the water table" choice ignores that the WT position affects pore pressure at all depths below it.

statement: A clay layer is drained on top (sand) and sits on impermeable rock at the bottom. The layer is 20 ft thick. What is the drainage path length $H_{dr}$ for computing the time factor $T_v$?
explanation: With sand on top (permeable) and rock on bottom (impermeable), water can only drain upward -- this is one-way drainage. For one-way drainage, $H_{dr}$ equals the full layer thickness: $H_{dr} = H = 20$ ft. The 10 ft choice would be correct for two-way drainage ($H_{dr} = H/2$), but that requires permeable boundaries on both sides. The 40 ft choice doubles the thickness for no reason. The 5 ft choice divides by 4, which is not a valid drainage path.

statement: A clay layer has $c_v = 0.40 \text{ ft}^2\text{/day}$ and two-way drainage with $H_{dr} = 8 \text{ ft}$. Using $T_v = 0.848$ for $U = 90\%$, how many days for 90% consolidation?
explanation: $t = T_v \times H_{dr}^2 / c_v = 0.848 \times 64 / 0.40 = 54.27 / 0.40 = 135.7 \approx 136$ days. The 542-day choice uses the full layer thickness $H = 16$ ft instead of $H_{dr} = 8$ ft (quadruples the time). The 17-day choice might divide by $H_{dr}$ instead of $H_{dr}^2$. The 68-day choice divides the correct answer by 2 for no reason.

statement: An overconsolidated clay has $p_0' = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$ and $p_c = 3{,}000 \text{ psf}$. A new fill increases stress by $\Delta\sigma = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$. Which consolidation case applies, and which compression index controls the settlement?

choices.text: Case 1 with $C_c$, because all consolidation uses the compression index
Case 2 (normally consolidated) with $C_c$, because the soil is being loaded
Case 1 (entirely in recompression) with $C_r$, because $p_0' + \Delta\sigma = 2{,}500 < p_c = 3{,}000$

explanation: The final stress is $p_0 + \Delta p = 1{,}500 + 1{,}000 = 2{,}500$ psf. Since $2{,}500 < p_c = 3{,}000$, the entire stress increase stays below the preconsolidation pressure. This is Case 1 -- entirely in the recompression range. The applicable index is $C_r$ (recompression), not $C_c$ (virgin compression). Case 2 applies only to NC clay ($p_0 \geq p_c$). Case 3 applies when the final stress crosses $p_c$ ($p_0 < p_c < p_0 + \Delta p$). The choice claiming Case 1 with $C_c$ is wrong because Case 1 uses $C_r$, not $C_c$.

statement: A granular soil ($c' = 0$) has an effective friction angle $\phi' = 35\degree$. What is the shear strength on a plane where the effective normal stress is $\sigma_N' = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$?
explanation: $\tau_f = c' + \sigma_N' \tan(\phi') = 0 + 2{,}000 \times \tan(35\degree) = 2{,}000 \times 0.7002 = 1{,}400$ psf. The 2,000 psf option is the normal stress, not the shear strength. The 1,148 psf option comes from using $\sin(35\degree)$ instead of $\tan(35\degree)$. The 700 psf option divides the answer by 2 for no reason.

statement: A saturated clay is loaded rapidly, and the engineer selects undrained parameters ($c_u$, $\phi_u = 0$). Which statement best describes why $\phi_u = 0$?

choices.text: Clay particles are flat and smooth, so there is no frictional resistance
Under undrained loading, excess pore pressure absorbs the stress change so effective stress on the failure plane does not change, making shear strength independent of applied normal stress
The friction angle is always zero for any clay soil regardless of drainage
Water between particles acts as a lubricant, eliminating all friction

explanation: In undrained loading of a saturated clay, any increase in total stress is carried entirely by excess pore water pressure. The effective stress on the failure plane stays the same, so the shear strength does not change with the applied confining pressure -- hence $\phi_u = 0$ in total-stress terms. The "flat smooth particles" choice is wrong because clay does have friction in drained conditions ($\phi'$ is typically 20-30 degrees). The "friction angle is always zero for any clay" choice is wrong because drained analysis uses nonzero $\phi'$. The "water acts as a lubricant" choice is a misconception -- water does not eliminate friction in the soil skeleton.

statement: A drained triaxial test on a cohesionless sand gives $\sigma_1' = 9{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and $\sigma_3' = 3{,}000 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the effective friction angle $\phi'$?
explanation: For $c = 0$: $\sin(\phi) = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/(\sigma_1 + \sigma_3) = (9{,}000 - 3{,}000)/(9{,}000 + 3{,}000) = 6{,}000/12{,}000 = 0.50$. $\phi = \arcsin(0.50) = 30\degree$. The 45 choice might come from computing the stress ratio $\sigma_1/\sigma_3 = 3$ and misusing it. The 26.6 choice is $\arctan(0.50)$ -- a common error from using tan instead of sin. The 19.5 choice might come from $\arcsin(\sigma_3/\sigma_1)$.

statement: Two UU triaxial tests on identical saturated clay specimens give the same undrained shear strength $c_u = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$, even though the confining pressures were $\sigma_3 = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and $\sigma_3 = 4{,}000 \text{ psf}$. Which explanation is most correct?

choices.text: The specimens consolidated under the higher pressure before shearing, so both reached the same strength
The tests were performed incorrectly; different confining pressures must produce different strengths
The clay was overconsolidated, which makes it insensitive to confining pressure
In a UU test on saturated clay ($\phi_u = 0$), the confining pressure generates equal excess pore pressure, so effective stress at failure is the same in both tests

explanation: In a UU test on saturated clay, the sample is not allowed to drain. Any increase in confining pressure goes entirely to pore pressure, so the effective stress does not change. Since strength depends on effective stress, both specimens have the same shear strength regardless of the confining pressure. This is why the Mohr envelope is a horizontal line ($\phi_u = 0$) with $\tau_f = c_u$. The "tests were performed incorrectly" choice is wrong -- this is exactly expected behavior. The "overconsolidated clay" choice is wrong -- even NC clays behave this way in UU tests. The "consolidated under the higher pressure" choice describes a CU or CD test, not UU.

statement: A strip footing is 1.5 m wide, founded at a depth of 1.0 m in a cohesive soil with $c = 80\,\text{kPa}$, $\phi = 0°$, and $\gamma = 18\,\text{kN/m}^3$. Using Terzaghi's equation with $N_c = 5.7$, $N_q = 1.0$, $N_\gamma = 0$, what is the ultimate bearing capacity?
explanation: For a strip footing: $q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5\gamma B N_\gamma$. With $\phi = 0$, $N_\gamma = 0$ so the third term drops out. $q$ (overburden) $= \gamma D = 18 \times 1.0 = 18$ kPa. $q_u = 80(5.7) + 18(1.0) + 0 = 456 + 18 = 474$ kPa. The trap is forgetting the overburden pressure term ($qN_q$).

statement: In Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation, increasing the depth of the footing primarily affects the bearing capacity through:
explanation: The overburden pressure $q = \gamma D_f$. When you increase the depth $D_f$, $q$ increases, which directly increases the $qN_q$ term. The cohesion term depends on soil properties (not depth), and the width term depends on footing width $B$ (not depth). So deeper footings have higher bearing capacity primarily because of the increased overburden.

statement: A strip footing is designed with a factor of safety of 3 against bearing capacity failure. If the water table rises from well below the footing to the ground surface, the allowable bearing capacity will:

choices.text: Increase because buoyancy reduces soil weight
Decrease because effective unit weight replaces total unit weight
Remain unchanged because the FS is the same
Decrease only if the soil is cohesionless

explanation: The bearing capacity equation uses the effective unit weight of the soil. When the water table rises to the surface, you replace the total unit weight with the buoyant unit weight ($\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w$), which is roughly half the original value. This reduces both the overburden term ($\gamma D_f N_q$) and the width term ($0.5\gamma B N_\gamma$), lowering $q_{ult}$ and therefore $q_{allow}$. This happens regardless of whether the soil has cohesion or not, because the $\gamma$ terms affect all soils.

statement: A rigid basement wall is poured against soil and cannot move. Which earth pressure condition applies?

choices.text: Active ($K_a$), because it is the minimum pressure
Passive ($K_p$), because the wall resists the soil
At-rest ($K_0$), because the wall does not move

explanation: The at-rest condition ($K_0$) applies when a wall is perfectly rigid and does not deflect. Active pressure ($K_a$) develops only when the wall moves away from the soil, allowing the soil to expand. Passive pressure ($K_p$) develops when the wall pushes into the soil. A rigid basement wall that cannot deform experiences at-rest pressure. The active choice is wrong because active requires the wall to move away from the soil. The passive choice is wrong because passive requires the wall to push into the soil. The "both active and passive simultaneously" choice is not a real condition.

statement: A 20-ft-tall retaining wall has backfill with $\phi' = 30\degree$, $\gamma = 110 \text{ pcf}$, and $c = 0$. What is the total active force per foot of wall?
explanation: $K_a = \tan^2(45\degree - 30\degree/2) = \tan^2(30\degree) = (1/\sqrt{3})^2 = 1/3 = 0.333$. $P_a = 0.5 \times K_a \times \gamma \times H^2 = 0.5 \times 0.333 \times 110 \times 400 = 7{,}333 \approx 7{,}330$ lb/ft. The 14,670 lb/ft option forgets the 1/2 factor. The 22,000 lb/ft option uses $K_p = 3$ instead of $K_a = 1/3$. The 3,670 lb/ft option halves the answer again incorrectly.

statement: A student computes $K_a = 2.5$ for a soil with $\phi' = 25\degree$. Which statement identifies the error?

choices.text: The student used degrees instead of radians in the calculator
The formula was applied correctly; $K_a = 2.5$ is reasonable
The student used $\tan^2(45\degree + \phi/2)$ instead of $\tan^2(45\degree - \phi/2)$, computing $K_p$ instead of $K_a$
The student forgot to square the tangent term

explanation: $K_a$ must always be less than 1 (active pressure is less than vertical stress). If $K_a = 2.5$, the student swapped the sign and computed $K_p$ instead. The correct $K_a = \tan^2(45\degree - 25\degree/2) = \tan^2(32.5\degree) = 0.406$. Check: $K_a \times K_p = 1$, so $K_p = 1/0.406 = 2.46 \approx 2.5$. The choice claiming $K_a = 2.5$ is reasonable is wrong because $K_a > 1$ is physically impossible for cohesionless soil. The degrees-vs-radians choice is unlikely to produce exactly 2.5. The forgot-to-square choice would give $\tan(32.5\degree) = 0.637$, not 2.5.

statement: A normally consolidated soil has $\phi' = 30\degree$. Compute both $K_a$ and $K_0$, and determine the ratio $K_0 / K_a$.
explanation: $K_a = \tan^2(45\degree - 15\degree) = \tan^2(30\degree) = 1/3 = 0.333$. $K_0 = 1 - \sin(30\degree) = 1 - 0.50 = 0.500$. Ratio $= 0.500/0.333 = 1.50$. This means a rigid wall ($K_0$) experiences 50% more force than a wall that can yield into the active condition ($K_a$). The $K_a=0.500, K_0=0.333$ option swaps $K_a$ and $K_0$. The $K_0=K_a=0.333$ option incorrectly assumes $K_0 = K_a$. The $K_0=0.577$ option uses $\tan(30\degree) = 0.577$ as $K_0$ instead of $1 - \sin(30\degree)$.

statement: A retaining wall has a total sliding resistance of $\Sigma F_R = 6{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$ and the horizontal driving force is $\Sigma F_D = 3{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
explanation: $FS_{sliding} = $ resisting forces / driving forces $= 6{,}000/3{,}000 = 2.0$. This is a direct ratio. The 0.50 option inverts the ratio (driving/resisting). The 3,000 option subtracts instead of dividing. The 1.0 option might come from thinking the forces are equal.

statement: For a gravity retaining wall, the resultant vertical force on the base has eccentricity $e = B/4$. What does this indicate about the base pressure distribution?

choices.text: The resultant is within the middle third, producing a trapezoidal distribution
The resultant is at the center of the base, producing uniform pressure
The resultant falls outside the middle third ($e > B/6$), so tension develops at the heel and the trapezoidal formula does not apply
The eccentricity has no effect on the pressure distribution

explanation: The middle-third rule says the resultant must fall within $B/6$ of the center for the entire base to be in compression. Here $e = B/4 = 0.25B$, and $B/6 = 0.167B$. Since $0.25B > 0.167B$, the resultant is outside the middle third. This means the heel side has theoretical tension, but soil cannot take tension, so the actual pressure redistributes to a triangular distribution on the toe side only. The "uniform pressure / resultant at center" choice applies only when $e = 0$. The "within the middle third, trapezoidal distribution" choice applies when $e \leq B/6$. The "eccentricity has no effect" choice is wrong because eccentricity directly controls the pressure distribution.

statement: A gravity retaining wall has $FS_{\text{overturning}} = 2.5$ and $FS_{\text{sliding}} = 1.2$. The minimum required FS values are 2.0 for overturning and 1.5 for sliding. Which stability check controls the design?

choices.text: Neither check controls because the wall passes overturning
Overturning controls because it has the larger required FS
Both checks pass because the actual FS values exceed 1.0
Sliding controls -- $FS_{\text{sliding}} = 1.2 < 1.5$ required, so the wall fails the sliding check even though overturning is adequate

explanation: You must check each failure mode against its own required FS. Overturning: $2.5 \geq 2.0$, so it passes. Sliding: $1.2 < 1.5$, so it fails. Even though overturning is fine, the wall is inadequate because sliding does not meet the minimum FS. You could add a key (shear key) at the base or widen the footing to increase sliding resistance. The "overturning controls because it has the larger required FS" choice ignores that each check has a different threshold. The "both checks pass because the actual FS values exceed 1.0" choice is wrong because $FS > 1.0$ is not sufficient -- each mode has a specific required FS. The "neither check controls because the wall passes overturning" choice incorrectly assumes passing one check means the wall is stable overall.

statement: A soil has hydraulic conductivity $k = 5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm/s}$ and a hydraulic gradient $i = 0.4$. What is the discharge velocity?
explanation: Discharge velocity v = ki = (5×10⁻⁴)(0.4) = 2.0×10⁻⁴ cm/s. The 1.25×10⁻³ choice divides by the gradient instead of multiplying. The 5×10⁻⁴ choice drops the gradient (uses k alone). The 2.0×10⁻³ choice is off by a factor of 10.

statement: A dry cohesionless slope is inclined at $\beta = 25\degree$ in a sand with friction angle $\phi = 38\degree$. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
explanation: Dry cohesionless infinite slope: FS = tan φ/tan β = tan 38°/tan 25° = 0.7813/0.4663 = 1.68. The 0.60 option inverts the ratio (tan β/tan φ). The 1.52 option subtracts angles. The 0.84 option applies an unneeded seepage reduction (multiplying by ~0.5).

statement: A compacted fill has a field dry unit weight of $112\text{ pcf}$. The standard Proctor maximum dry unit weight is $118\text{ pcf}$. What is the relative compaction?
explanation: RC = (γd,field/γd,max) × 100 = (112/118) × 100 = 94.9%. The 105.4% choice inverts the ratio (118/112). The 5.4% choice is the difference relative to the field value (6/112). The 88.0% choice is an unrelated guess. This fill is just below a typical 95% requirement.

statement: A pile develops $Q_p = 350\text{ kN}$ of end bearing and $Q_s = 450\text{ kN}$ of skin friction. Using a factor of safety of $2.5$, what is the allowable pile load?
explanation: Ultimate capacity Q_ult = Qp + Qs = 350 + 450 = 800 kN. Allowable = Q_ult/FS = 800/2.5 = 320 kN. The 800 kN option forgets to divide by the factor of safety. The 140 kN option divides only the end bearing (350/2.5). The 2,000 kN option multiplies by the FS instead of dividing.

statement: A soil has dry unit weight $\gamma_d = 100 \text{ pcf}$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.68$. What is the void ratio $e$?
explanation: Dry unit weight relates to void ratio by $\gamma_d = G_s \gamma_w / (1+e)$. Solve for e: $e = G_s \gamma_w/\gamma_d - 1 = 2.68 \times 62.4/100 - 1 = 1.672 - 1 = 0.672$. The 1.672 distractor forgot to subtract 1 (that is the (1+e) value). The 0.401 distractor is the porosity $n = e/(1+e)$, not the void ratio. The 0.602 distractor comes from using a rounded or wrong unit weight of water.

statement: A clay has void ratio $e = 0.85$, $G_s = 2.72$, and degree of saturation $S = 60\%$. What is the total (moist) unit weight?
explanation: Total unit weight is $\gamma = (G_s + Se)\gamma_w/(1+e)$. Here $Se = 0.60 \times 0.85 = 0.51$, so $\gamma = (2.72 + 0.51)(62.4)/(1.85) = 3.23 \times 62.4/1.85 = 201.6/1.85 = 108.9$ pcf. The 91.8 value is the dry unit weight $G_s\gamma_w/(1+e)$, dropping the Se term. The 120.9 value uses the saturated formula $(G_s+e)\gamma_w/(1+e)$, treating S as 1. The 98.7 value comes from using a partial Se contribution.

statement: A fine-grained soil has $LL = 35$ and $PL = 18$, with 65% passing the No. 200 sieve. The A-line value at $LL = 35$ is $PI_A = 0.73(35-20) = 10.95$. What is the USCS classification?
explanation: First $PI = LL - PL = 35 - 18 = 17$. The soil is fine-grained ($65\% > 50\%$ passes #200) with $LL = 35 < 50$ (low plasticity, L). The A-line at $LL = 35$ is $PI_A = 10.95$. Since $PI = 17 > 10.95$, the soil plots above the A-line, so it is a clay (C). Classification: CL. The ML option would require plotting below the A-line. The CH option requires $LL \geq 50$. The SC option is a coarse-grained soil with clay fines.

statement: A gravel has $D_{10} = 0.40 \text{ mm}$, $D_{30} = 2.4 \text{ mm}$, $D_{60} = 8.0 \text{ mm}$, with less than 5% fines and more than half the coarse fraction retained on the No. 4 sieve. What is the USCS classification?
explanation: Coarse-grained, gravel (G) since more than half the coarse fraction is retained on No. 4. With < 5% fines, classify by gradation. $C_u = D_{60}/D_{10} = 8.0/0.40 = 20$ (gravel needs $\geq 4$, passes). $C_c = (D_{30})^2/(D_{10} D_{60}) = (2.4)^2/(0.40 \times 8.0) = 5.76/3.20 = 1.80$ (need 1–3, passes). Both pass → well-graded gravel, GW. The GP option would apply if a gradation criterion failed. The SW option misidentifies it as sand. The GM option requires more than 12% fines.

statement: A profile has 4 ft of moist sand ($\gamma = 118 \text{ pcf}$) above the water table, then saturated sand ($\gamma_{sat} = 128 \text{ pcf}$) below it. What is the effective vertical stress at a point 6 ft below the water table?
explanation: Total stress: $\sigma = 118(4) + 128(6) = 472 + 768 = 1{,}240$ psf. Pore pressure (6 ft below WT): $u = 62.4(6) = 374$ psf. Effective: $\sigma' = 1{,}240 - 374 = 866 \approx 865$ psf. Or use buoyant weight: $\sigma' = 118(4) + (128-62.4)(6) = 472 + 393.6 = 865.6$ psf. The 1,240 value is the total stress without subtracting pore pressure. The 394 value is only the buoyant contribution of the saturated zone, missing the moist sand overburden. The 766 value comes from an error in handling the pore pressure or zone thickness; it does not match either the correct method (865 psf) or the listed partial methods.

statement: At a depth of 15 ft in a saturated clay, the total vertical stress is $\sigma = 1{,}800 \text{ psf}$. An artesian condition raises the piezometric head to 3 ft ABOVE the ground surface, so the water column acting at this point is 18 ft. What is the effective vertical stress?
explanation: Under artesian pressure the pore pressure uses the full piezometric head, not just the depth. Head = 15 ft depth + 3 ft above surface = 18 ft. $u = \gamma_w h = 62.4 \times 18 = 1{,}123$ psf. Effective stress: $\sigma' = \sigma - u = 1{,}800 - 1{,}123 = 677$ psf. The 1,123 psf choice is the pore pressure itself. The 864 psf choice uses only the 15 ft depth ($u = 62.4 \times 15 = 936$, giving $1{,}800 - 936 = 864$), ignoring the artesian head. The 1,800 psf choice forgets to subtract pore pressure entirely.

statement: A clay layer reaches $U = 50\%$ consolidation in 40 days ($T_v = 0.197$ at $U = 50\%$). For the same layer and drainage conditions, how long until $U = 90\%$? Use $T_v = 0.848$ at $U = 90\%$.
explanation: Because $c_v$ and $H_{dr}$ are fixed, time is proportional to the time factor: $t_2/t_1 = T_{v2}/T_{v1}$. So $t_{90} = t_{50} \times (T_{v90}/T_{v50}) = 40 \times (0.848/0.197) = 40 \times 4.305 = 172$ days. The 72 value scales by the ratio of U values (90/50 = 1.8) instead of the time-factor ratio. The 9 value inverts the ratio. The 340 value roughly doubles the correct answer.

statement: A soil has $c' = 150 \text{ psf}$ and $\phi' = 28\degree$. On a potential failure plane the mobilized shear stress is $\tau = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and the effective normal stress is $\sigma_N' = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$. What is the factor of safety against shear failure on this plane?
explanation: Available strength: $\tau_f = c' + \sigma_N' \tan\phi' = 150 + 2{,}000 \tan 28\degree = 150 + 2{,}000(0.5317) = 150 + 1{,}063 = 1{,}213$ psf. FS = strength/mobilized = $1{,}213/1{,}000 = 1.21$. The 1.06 choice drops the cohesion term ($1{,}063/1{,}000$). The 0.82 choice inverts the ratio ($1{,}000/1{,}213$). The 2.13 choice forgets to multiply the normal stress by tan, adding $\sigma_N'$ directly.

statement: A 16-ft-tall basement wall is rigid and does not move. The backfill is normally consolidated sand with $\phi' = 32\degree$, $\gamma = 115 \text{ pcf}$, $c = 0$. What is the total at-rest lateral force per foot of wall?
explanation: A rigid wall uses the at-rest coefficient $K_0 = 1 - \sin\phi = 1 - \sin 32\degree = 1 - 0.530 = 0.470$. Total force: $P_0 = 0.5 K_0 \gamma H^2 = 0.5(0.470)(115)(16^2) = 0.5(0.470)(115)(256) = 6{,}919 \approx 6{,}920$ lb/ft. The 4,520 value uses the active coefficient $K_a = \tan^2(45-16) = 0.307$ instead of $K_0$. The 13,840 value forgets the 1/2 factor. The 3,460 value halves the answer an extra time.

statement: A wall retains a purely cohesive backfill in the undrained condition with $c_u = 400 \text{ psf}$, $\phi_u = 0$, $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$. With $\phi = 0$, $K_a = 1$ and the active pressure is $\sigma_a = \gamma z - 2c_u$. At what depth $z_c$ does the active pressure first become positive (the tension crack depth)?
explanation: For $\phi_u = 0$, $K_a = 1$ and the active pressure is $\sigma_a = \gamma z - 2c_u$. Setting $\sigma_a = 0$: $z_c = 2c_u/\gamma = 2(400)/120 = 800/120 = 6.7$ ft. The 3.3 value drops the factor of 2 ($c_u/\gamma = 400/120$). The 13.3 value uses $4c_u/\gamma$, doubling the factor by mistake. The 0.3 value inverts the ratio ($\gamma/(2c_u)$-style error).

statement: A gravity retaining wall resists sliding through base friction. The total vertical force is $\Sigma V = 12{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$, the base friction coefficient is $\mu = \tan\delta = 0.55$, and the horizontal driving force (active thrust) is $\Sigma F_D = 4{,}800 \text{ lb/ft}$. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
explanation: Sliding resistance is base friction: $\Sigma F_R = \mu \Sigma V = 0.55 \times 12{,}000 = 6{,}600$ lb/ft. FS = resisting/driving = $6{,}600/4{,}800 = 1.38$. The 2.50 value divides $\Sigma V$ by $\Sigma F_D$ directly, forgetting to multiply by mu. The 0.73 value inverts the correct ratio. The 0.40 value divides driving by vertical without the friction term.

statement: A retaining wall base is $B = 9 \text{ ft}$ wide, carries $\Sigma V = 9{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$, and the resultant has eccentricity $e = 1.0 \text{ ft}$ from the center. What is the minimum (heel) base pressure?
explanation: Check the middle third: $B/6 = 9/6 = 1.5$ ft. Since $e = 1.0 < 1.5$, the resultant is inside the middle third, so the full base is in compression and the trapezoidal formula applies. Minimum (heel) pressure: $q_{min} = (\Sigma V/B)(1 - 6e/B) = (9{,}000/9)(1 - 6(1.0)/9) = 1{,}000(1 - 0.667) = 1{,}000(0.333) = 333$ psf. The 1,000 psf option is the uniform pressure $\Sigma V/B$, ignoring eccentricity. The 1,667 psf option is the maximum (toe) pressure $q_{max} = 1{,}000(1 + 0.667)$. The 0 psf option wrongly assumes the resultant falls outside the middle third.

statement: A strip footing carries a working line load of $30{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$ over a width $B = 5 \text{ ft}$. The ultimate bearing capacity is $q_{ult} = 18{,}000 \text{ psf}$. What is the actual factor of safety against a bearing failure?
explanation: Applied bearing pressure = load / area = $30{,}000 / 5 = 6{,}000$ psf (per foot of strip length). FS = $q_{ult}/q_{applied} = 18{,}000/6{,}000 = 3.0$. The 0.6 value compares $q_{ult}$ to the total line load $30{,}000$ instead of the contact pressure ($18{,}000/30{,}000$). The 1.5 value divides by the half-width $B/2 = 2.5$ ft instead of the full width ($q = 30{,}000/2.5 = 12{,}000$, giving $18{,}000/12{,}000 = 1.5$). The 6.0 value uses twice the width ($q = 30{,}000/10 = 3{,}000$, giving $18{,}000/3{,}000 = 6.0$).

statement: A flow net beneath a sheet pile has $N_f = 5$ flow channels and $N_d = 10$ equipotential drops. With $k = 1 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$ and a total head loss of $H = 8\text{ m}$, what is the seepage per unit width?
explanation: q = kH(Nf/Nd) = (1×10⁻⁴)(8)(5/10) = (1×10⁻⁴)(8)(0.5) = 4.0×10⁻⁴ m³/s per m. The 1.6×10⁻³ option inverts the ratio (uses Nd/Nf = 2). The 8.0×10⁻⁴ option drops the ratio (uses 1.0). The 2.0×10⁻⁴ option halves the head (uses H = 4).

statement: A dry cohesionless sand slope stands stably at the angle of repose. After a prolonged rainfall produces steady seepage parallel to the slope, what happens to the factor of safety?

choices.text: It drops to roughly half its dry value (factor γ′/γ_sat ≈ 0.5)
It is unchanged, because friction angle is unaffected by water
It roughly doubles because water adds weight and stability

explanation: Seepage parallel to a cohesionless slope multiplies the factor of safety by γ′/γ_sat ≈ 0.5, so a slope at FS ≈ 1.0 dry can drop to ≈ 0.5 and fail. The "unchanged" choice ignores the buoyancy/seepage effect on effective stress. The "roughly doubles" choice has the direction backwards. The "becomes infinite" choice is nonsensical.

statement: A sand has $e_{max} = 0.80$, $e_{min} = 0.45$, and an in-place void ratio $e = 0.52$. What is its relative density?
explanation: Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100 = (0.80 − 0.52)/(0.80 − 0.45) × 100 = 0.28/0.35 × 100 = 80% — a dense sand. The 20% choice uses (e − emin) in the numerator. The 65% choice miscomputes the denominator. The 35% choice inverts the numerator.

statement: A driven pile reaches refusal on sound rock after passing through soft soils. How does it primarily carry its load?

choices.text: Mostly by end bearing at the tip on the rock
Mostly by skin friction in the soft soils
Equally by end bearing and negative skin friction
By buoyancy from the surrounding soil

explanation: A pile bearing on sound rock acts essentially as an end-bearing pile — the strong tip support dominates, while the soft soils contribute little skin friction. The "skin friction in the soft soils" option describes a friction pile in deep uniform soil. The "equally by end bearing and negative skin friction" option invents a role for downdrag. The "buoyancy" option is not a real load-carrying mechanism here.

statement: A road carries $1{,}200 \text{ veh/hr}$. The peak 15-minute volume within that hour is $400 \text{ veh}$. What is the peak 15-minute flow rate?
explanation: The peak flow rate extrapolates the worst 15 minutes to an hourly rate: 4 × V₁₅ = 4 × 400 = 1,600 veh/hr. Equivalently, PHF = V/(4×V₁₅) = 1,200/1,600 = 0.75, and flow rate = V/PHF = 1,200/0.75 = 1,600. The tricky part: the flow rate is HIGHER than the hourly volume because it represents the peak surge. The 1,200 veh/hr choice is the hourly volume itself — that is the demand, not the peak rate. The 400 veh/hr choice is V₁₅ without multiplying by 4. The 900 veh/hr choice multiplied V × PHF instead of dividing.

statement: A crest vertical curve has $A = 8$ and required stopping sight distance $S = 500 \text{ ft}$. Assuming $S \leq L$, what is the minimum curve length?
explanation: Direct plug-in: L = AS²/2,158 = 8 × 500²/2,158 = 8 × 250,000/2,158 = 2,000,000/2,158 = 927 ft. Check: S = 500 < L = 927, so S ≤ L is satisfied. The 500 ft choice confused L with S. The 730 ft choice used the S > L formula (2×500 − 2,158/8 = 1,000 − 270 = 730). The 464 ft choice used A/2 = 4 instead of 8.

statement: A crest vertical curve connects a $+3\%$ grade to a $-5\%$ grade with curve length $L = 800 \text{ ft}$. What is the tangent offset $E$ at the PVI?
explanation: E = (g₂ − g₁) × L/8. Convert grades to decimals: g₁ = +0.03, g₂ = −0.05. E = (−0.05 − 0.03) × 800/8 = −0.08 × 100 = −8.0 ft. The magnitude is 8.0 ft. The negative sign means the curve dips below the tangent line (crest). The 16 ft choice used L/4 instead of L/8. The 4 ft choice used L/16. The 32 ft choice used L/2.

statement: A horizontal curve has a degree of curve $D = 6\degree$. What is the curve radius?
explanation: R = 5,729.58/D = 5,729.58/6 = 954.9 ≈ 955 ft. Direct division. The 5,730 ft option forgot to divide by D (used D = 1). The 34,377 ft option multiplied instead of dividing: 5,729.58 × 6 = 34,377. The 478 ft option divided by 12 instead of 6.

statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 1{,}200 \text{ ft}$ and intersection angle $I = 30\degree$. What is the tangent distance $T$?
explanation: T = R tan(I/2) = 1,200 × tan(15°) = 1,200 × 0.2679 = 321.5 ≈ 322 ft. The 693 ft choice used tan(I) = tan(30°) = 0.5774 instead of tan(I/2) — forgot to halve the angle: 1,200 × 0.5774 = 693. The 628 ft choice is the curve length L = RI(π/180) = 1,200 × 30 × π/180 = 628 — confused T with L. The 161 ft choice divided by 2 one too many times.

statement: An intersection approach has a speed of $50 \text{ mph}$. Using driver reaction time $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and deceleration $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$ on a level grade, what is the yellow interval?
explanation: First convert 50 mph to ft/sec: 50 × 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. Then y = t + v/(2a) = 1.0 + 73.3/(2 × 10) = 1.0 + 73.3/20 = 1.0 + 3.67 = 4.67 ≈ 4.7 sec. The 3.5 sec option used mph directly: 1.0 + 50/20 = 3.5 — forgot to convert to ft/sec. The 3.7 sec option forgot the reaction time: 73.3/20 = 3.67. The 8.3 sec option used v/a instead of v/(2a): 1.0 + 73.3/10 = 8.3.

statement: An intersection is $60 \text{ ft}$ wide (curb to curb). A design vehicle is $20 \text{ ft}$ long and approaches at $50 \text{ mph}$. What is the all-red clearance interval?
explanation: Convert speed: 50 × 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. r = (W + l)/v = (60 + 20)/73.3 = 80/73.3 = 1.09 ≈ 1.1 sec. The 1.6 sec choice used mph instead of ft/sec: 80/50 = 1.6. The 0.8 sec choice forgot the vehicle length: 60/73.3 = 0.82. The 0.9 sec choice inverted and divided v by (W+l).

statement: A freeway has free-flow speed $S_f = 70 \text{ mph}$ and jam density $D_j = 180 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. Using the Greenshields model, what is the maximum flow?
explanation: Vm = DjSf/4 = 180 × 70/4 = 12,600/4 = 3,150 veh/hr/ln. Direct formula application. The 12,600 option forgot to divide by 4: Dj × Sf = 12,600. The 6,300 option divided by 2 instead of 4. The 1,575 option divided by 8 instead of 4.

statement: A road has $S_f = 60 \text{ mph}$ and $D_j = 120 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. What is the speed when density is $D = 40 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$?
explanation: S = Sf − (Sf/Dj) × D = 60 − (60/120) × 40 = 60 − 0.5 × 40 = 60 − 20 = 40 mph. The 60 mph choice used Sf directly without the density reduction. The 20 mph choice computed only the reduction term (Sf/Dj × D = 20) and forgot to subtract from Sf. The 30 mph choice is the optimum speed So = Sf/2, which occurs at D = Dj/2 = 60, not at D = 40.

statement: A freeway has $10\%$ trucks ($P_T = 0.10$) on level terrain ($E_T = 2.0$). What is the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor $f_{HV}$?
explanation: fHV = 1/(1 + PT(ET − 1)) = 1/(1 + 0.10(2.0 − 1)) = 1/(1 + 0.10) = 1/1.10 = 0.909. The 0.833 option used rolling terrain ET = 3.0: 1/(1 + 0.10 × 2) = 1/1.20. The 1.100 option inverted the formula and got the denominator itself. The 0.800 option used PT × ET = 0.20, then 1 − 0.20 = 0.80.

statement: A 3-lane directional freeway carries $V = 4{,}500 \text{ veh/hr}$ with $PHF = 0.92$ and $f_{HV} = 0.909$. What is the demand flow rate $v_p$?
explanation: vp = V/(PHF × N × fHV) = 4,500/(0.92 × 3 × 0.909) = 4,500/2.509 = 1,793 pc/h/ln. All three adjustments (PHF, lanes, heavy vehicles) must be applied. The 1,630 pc/h/ln choice forgot fHV: 4,500/(0.92 × 3) = 4,500/2.76 = 1,630. The 1,650 pc/h/ln choice forgot PHF: 4,500/(3 × 0.909) = 4,500/2.73 = 1,650. The 4,500 pc/h/ln choice applied no adjustments at all.

statement: In the four-step travel demand model, which step uses the gravity model?
explanation: The gravity model distributes the trips produced by each zone among destination zones — that is trip DISTRIBUTION (step 2). Trip generation (step 1) just counts productions and attractions; mode choice (step 3) splits trips among modes; traffic assignment (step 4) loads trips onto routes.

statement: In the gravity model, as the travel time (impedance) between two zones increases, the number of trips distributed between them generally:

choices.text: Decreases, because the friction factor decreases
Increases, because the friction factor increases
Stays the same — only attractions matter
Depends only on the number of productions

explanation: The friction factor F decreases as travel time or distance grows, so more-distant zones receive fewer trips — just as gravitational attraction weakens with distance. The "increases because the friction factor increases" choice reverses this. The "only attractions matter" and "depends only on productions" choices ignore the impedance term entirely.

statement: A yellow, diamond-shaped sign warning of a curve ahead belongs to which category of traffic control device?
explanation: Yellow diamond-shaped signs are WARNING signs — they alert drivers to conditions ahead such as curves, intersections, or merges. Regulatory signs state laws (STOP, speed limit). Guide signs are green and give directions. A construction barricade is a temporary-traffic-control device, not this sign.

statement: Why does the MUTCD require a warrant analysis before a traffic signal is installed at an intersection?

choices.text: Because an unwarranted signal can increase rear-end crashes and delay; a signal must be justified
Because signals always reduce all types of crashes
Because warrants set the signal’s cycle length
Because federal law bans all signals without a permit fee

explanation: Signals are not automatically beneficial — installing one where it is not warranted can raise rear-end crashes and create unnecessary delay. Warrants test whether conditions (volumes, pedestrians, crashes) justify a signal. The claim that signals always reduce all types of crashes is false (signals can increase some crash types, like rear-end). The option about cycle length confuses warrants with timing design. The federal permit-fee option is fabricated.

statement: A STOP sign is an example of which category of traffic control device?
explanation: A STOP sign imposes a legal requirement — drivers must stop — so it is a REGULATORY sign (the distinctive red octagon is reserved for STOP). Warning signs (yellow diamonds) alert to conditions; guide signs (green) give directions; recreational signs mark parks and points of interest.

statement: A road receives $1{,}000$ passes of a $24{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single-axle load per year. The load equivalency factor for a $24{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single axle is $3.03$. How many ESALs does this produce annually?
explanation: ESALs = passes × LEF = 1,000 × 3.03 = 3,030. Each pass of a 24-kip single axle does 3.03 times the damage of a standard 18-kip axle. The 260 choice used the tandem-axle LEF (0.260) instead of the single-axle LEF (3.03) — always check single vs. tandem in the table. The 1,000 choice assumed LEF = 1.0 (only true for an 18-kip axle). The 24,000 choice multiplied by the axle weight instead of the LEF.

statement: Two cross sections are $100 \text{ ft}$ apart with areas $A_1 = 200 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 300 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the earthwork volume using the average end area method?
explanation: V = L(A1 + A2)/2 = 100(200 + 300)/2 = 100 × 250 = 25,000 ft³. Convert: 25,000/27 = 926 yd³. The 1,852 yd³ option forgot to divide by 2 in the average: 100 × 500/27 = 1,852. The 25,000 option is the answer in ft³, not yd³ — forgot to divide by 27. The 741 yd³ option used only A1: 100 × 200/27 = 741.

statement: How does a rigid (PCC) pavement primarily distribute wheel loads to the subgrade, compared with a flexible (asphalt) pavement?

choices.text: By beam/slab action, spreading the load over a wide subgrade area
By flexing and transmitting load downward through granular layers
By concentrating the load directly beneath the wheel
It does not transmit load to the subgrade at all

explanation: A rigid slab is stiff and bends like a beam, spreading each wheel load over a wide area of subgrade — so it depends less on subgrade strength. The "flexing and transmitting load through granular layers" option describes flexible (asphalt) pavement. The "concentrating the load directly beneath the wheel" option is the opposite of what a slab does. The "does not transmit load to the subgrade at all" option is incorrect — load still reaches the subgrade, just spread out.

statement: What is the primary purpose of dowel bars placed across transverse joints in a rigid pavement?

choices.text: To transfer wheel load between adjacent slabs while allowing movement
To bond the slabs together so they cannot move
To increase the concrete’s compressive strength

explanation: Dowel bars span a transverse joint and transfer wheel load from one slab to the next, reducing faulting, while still letting the slabs expand and contract. "Bond the slabs together so they cannot move" describes tie bars (which hold longitudinal joints closed). "Increase the concrete's compressive strength" confuses dowels with reinforcement. "Waterproof the joint" is the job of joint sealant, not dowels.

statement: The modulus of subgrade reaction ($k$) used in rigid pavement design represents:

choices.text: The pressure required to produce a unit deflection of the subgrade
The flexural strength of the concrete slab
The total thickness of the pavement structure
The number of equivalent single-axle loads

explanation: The modulus of subgrade reaction k is the foundation stiffness — pressure per unit deflection (e.g., pci) — describing how firmly the subgrade supports the slab. The flexural-strength option is the concrete’s modulus of rupture. The total-thickness option is a thickness, not a stiffness. The equivalent-single-axle-loads option is the ESAL traffic measure.

statement: A road has a design speed of $45 \text{ mph}$ on a level grade. Using $t = 2.5 \text{ s}$ and $a = 11.2 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the braking distance component of the SSD?
explanation: Braking distance $= V^2 / [30(a/32.2 \pm G)]$. On a level grade $G = 0$, so it simplifies to $V^2 / [30(a/32.2)] = 45^2 / [30(11.2/32.2)] = 2{,}025 / [30 \times 0.3478] = 2{,}025 / 10.43 = 194.1$ ft. The 165 ft choice used $a = 11.2$ directly in the denominator without dividing by 32.2: $2{,}025/(30 \times 0.3733)$ is wrong. The 359 ft choice added the reaction distance when the question only asks for braking. The 388 ft choice divided by $2 \times 0.3478 \times 7.5$ incorrectly.

statement: A designer is computing SSD for a road with a $6\%$ upgrade. Compared to a level road at the same design speed, what happens to the SSD?

choices.text: SSD increases because gravity resists braking on an uphill grade
SSD decreases because gravity assists braking on an uphill grade
SSD is unchanged because grade does not affect braking distance
SSD decreases because drivers react faster going uphill

explanation: On an uphill grade, gravity pulls the vehicle backward, helping the brakes slow it down. In the formula, a positive $G$ makes the denominator $30(a/32.2 + G)$ larger, which makes the braking distance fraction smaller. The reaction distance is unchanged (grade does not affect perception-reaction time), but the braking distance is shorter. The choice claiming SSD increases reverses the effect of uphill. The "unchanged" choice ignores the grade term entirely. The "drivers react faster" choice wrongly claims grade affects reaction time.

statement: The major road at an intersection has a design speed of $50 \text{ mph}$. The time gap for a vehicle turning from the minor road is $t_g = 7.5 \text{ sec}$. What is the intersection sight distance (ISD)?
explanation: $ISD = 1.47 \times V_{\text{major}} \times t_g = 1.47 \times 50 \times 7.5 = 551.25$, which rounds to 551 ft. The 375 ft choice used mph directly without converting: $50 \times 7.5 = 375$. The 735 ft choice used $t_g = 10$ sec instead of 7.5 sec. The 110 ft choice forgot to multiply by $t_g$: $1.47 \times 50 \times 1.5 = 110$.

statement: A roadway carries $1{,}800 \text{ veh/hr}$ with a peak 15-minute count of $500 \text{ veh}$. An engineer reports the PHF as $0.90$ and the peak flow rate as $1{,}620 \text{ veh/hr}$. What error did the engineer make?

choices.text: The engineer multiplied V by PHF instead of dividing -- the correct flow rate is 2,000 veh/hr
The PHF calculation is wrong -- it should be 1.11, not 0.90
The engineer forgot to multiply by 4 -- the correct flow rate is 7,200 veh/hr
No error was made -- 1,620 veh/hr is correct

explanation: $PHF = V/(4 \times V_{15}) = 1{,}800/(4 \times 500) = 1{,}800/2{,}000 = 0.90$. That part is correct. The peak flow rate $= V/PHF = 1{,}800/0.90 = 2{,}000$ veh/hr (equivalently, $4 \times V_{15} = 2{,}000$). The engineer computed $1{,}800 \times 0.90 = 1{,}620$, which is $V$ times $PHF$ instead of $V$ divided by $PHF$. The flow rate should always be greater than or equal to the hourly volume, never less. Getting $1{,}620 < 1{,}800$ should have been a red flag. The choice claiming the PHF should be 1.11 is wrong because 0.90 is the correct PHF. The choice multiplying by 4 to get 7,200 veh/hr gives a nonsensical rate. The "no error was made" choice accepts the error.

statement: A crest vertical curve connects a $+2\%$ grade to a $-4\%$ grade with a curve length $L = 600 \text{ ft}$. What is the K-value (rate of vertical curvature)?
explanation: $A = |g_2 - g_1| \times 100 = |-0.04 - 0.02| \times 100 = 0.06 \times 100 = 6$. $K = L/A = 600/6 = 100$ ft per percent change. The 300 choice used $A = 2$ (only the magnitude of one grade, $L/2 = 300$). The 50 choice used $A = 12$ ($L/12 = 50$). The 6 choice confused $K$ with $A$ (it is just the algebraic difference, not the rate).

statement: When computing the minimum length of a sag vertical curve, the headlight criterion is used instead of the driver eye height criterion used for crest curves. Why?

choices.text: Sag curves are always shorter than crest curves, so a less restrictive criterion is needed
On a sag curve at night, the line of sight is not blocked by the road surface -- the limiting factor is how far the headlights illuminate the road ahead
The driver eye height is irrelevant on sag curves because the driver can always see over the curve
Headlights are only used at night, so the sag curve criterion applies only to nighttime design

explanation: On a crest curve, the road surface itself blocks the driver from seeing objects beyond the hill -- so the sight distance depends on eye height and object height. On a sag curve, you can see over the valley during the day with no obstruction. But at night, you can only see as far as your headlights illuminate. The headlight beam angle (about 1 degree upward) and the mounting height determine how far down the sag the beam reaches. The "sag curves are always shorter" choice is wrong because that is simply untrue. The "driver can always see over the curve" choice is incomplete -- it only addresses daytime. The "applies only to nighttime design" choice is wrong because the nighttime case is precisely what governs the design.

statement: A crest vertical curve is designed using the $S \leq L$ formula, but after computing $L$, the engineer finds that $S > L$. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Accept the result because the $S \leq L$ formula always gives a conservative (longer) answer
Average the results from both formulas for a more accurate answer
Double the computed $L$ to ensure adequate sight distance

explanation: The two formulas are derived under different geometric assumptions. The $S \leq L$ formula assumes the sight line stays within the curve limits, and the $S > L$ formula assumes the sight line extends beyond the curve ends. If you use $S \leq L$ and get $L < S$, the assumption is violated, so the result is not valid. You must switch to $L = 2S - 2{,}158/A$. The "accept the conservative result" choice is wrong — the $S \leq L$ formula does not always give a longer curve. In fact, when $S > L$ actually holds, the $S \leq L$ formula can give a shorter $L$. The "average both formulas" choice has no theoretical basis. The "double the computed $L$" choice is arbitrary.

statement: A horizontal curve has a radius $R = 1{,}146 \text{ ft}$. What is the degree of curve $D$?
explanation: $D = 5{,}729.58/R = 5{,}729.58/1{,}146 = 5.0$ degrees. This is the inverse of $R = 5{,}729.58/D$. The 0.20 choice divided $R$ by 5,729.58 instead of the other way around. The 10 choice used $R = 573$ (off by a factor of 2). The 2.5 choice doubled $R$ in the denominator.

statement: On a horizontal curve, the tangent distance formula is $T = R \tan(I/2)$. If an engineer mistakenly uses $\tan(I)$ instead of $\tan(I/2)$, what is the effect on the computed tangent distance?

choices.text: The computed T will be too small, leading to an underestimate of the tangent length
The computed T will be too large, leading to an overestimate of the tangent length
No effect because $\tan(I) = 2\tan(I/2)$ for all angles
The effect depends on whether $I$ is greater or less than $90\degree$

explanation: For any angle $I$ between 0 and 180 degrees (realistic for curves), $\tan(I) > \tan(I/2)$ since the tangent function is increasing on $(0\degree, 90\degree)$ and $I/2 < I$. So using $\tan(I)$ gives a larger number, making $T$ too large. The "too small / underestimate" choice gets the direction wrong. The "no effect because $\tan(I) = 2\tan(I/2)$" choice states a false identity -- $\tan(I)$ is NOT equal to $2\tan(I/2)$ in general. The "depends on whether $I$ is greater or less than $90\degree$" choice is wrong because for typical highway intersection angles (well under $90\degree$), the effect is always an overestimate.

statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 800 \text{ ft}$ and intersection angle $I = 50\degree$. What is the curve length $L$?
explanation: $L = R \times I \times (\pi/180) = 800 \times 50 \times (\pi/180) = 800 \times 0.8727 = 698$ ft. The 373 ft choice is the tangent distance $T = R\tan(I/2) = 800 \times \tan(25\degree) = 373$, not the curve length. The 466 ft choice incorrectly used a modified radian conversion. The 1,396 ft choice doubled the curve length for no reason: $2 \times 698$.

statement: A curve with design speed $V = 55 \text{ mph}$, radius $R = 900 \text{ ft}$, and superelevation $e = 6\%$ is analyzed. If the side friction demand exceeds the available friction factor $f$, what does this indicate about the design?

choices.text: The curve radius is too tight for the design speed and superelevation -- vehicles may slide outward
The curve is overdesigned and the radius should be reduced
The superelevation is too high and should be lowered
The design is acceptable because friction demand varies with weather

explanation: From $0.01e + f = V^2/(15R)$, the required side friction is $f = V^2/(15R) - 0.01e = 55^2/(15 \times 900) - 0.06 = 3{,}025/13{,}500 - 0.06 = 0.224 - 0.06 = 0.164$. Typical max $f$ values for 55 mph are around 0.13--0.14. If the demand (0.164) exceeds the supply, vehicles cannot maintain the curve at that speed without skidding outward. The fix is a larger radius, lower speed, or higher superelevation. The choice to reduce the radius makes the problem worse (smaller R raises V^2/15R). The choice to reduce superelevation also worsens friction demand. The choice claiming the design is acceptable dismisses a real safety concern.

statement: An approach has a speed of $40 \text{ mph}$ on a level grade. Using $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the yellow interval?
explanation: Convert 40 mph to ft/sec: $40 \times 1.467 = 58.7$ ft/sec. Then $y = t + v/(2a) = 1.0 + 58.7/(2 \times 10) = 1.0 + 58.7/20 = 1.0 + 2.93 = 3.93$, which rounds to 3.9 sec. The 3.0 sec choice used mph directly: $1.0 + 40/20 = 3.0$. The 6.9 sec choice used $v/a$ instead of $v/(2a)$: $1.0 + 58.7/10 = 6.87$. The 2.9 sec choice forgot the reaction time: $58.7/20 = 2.93$.

statement: The all-red clearance interval formula is $r = (W + l)/v$. Why is the vehicle length $l$ included in the numerator?

choices.text: The vehicle length accounts for the acceleration distance needed to enter the intersection
The vehicle must travel the full intersection width plus its own length to completely clear the far side before conflicting traffic enters
The vehicle length is a safety buffer added to account for driver hesitation
The vehicle length adjusts for the distance between the stop bar and the curb line

explanation: When the signal turns red, a vehicle that just entered must cross the entire intersection width $W$ before the conflicting phase starts. But the vehicle is not a point -- the rear bumper must also clear the far side. So the total clearance distance is $W$ (intersection width) plus $l$ (vehicle length). If you only used $W$, the tail end of the vehicle would still be in the intersection when cross traffic gets the green. The acceleration-distance choice confuses clearance with acceleration. The driver-hesitation safety-buffer choice has no basis in the formula derivation. The stop-bar-to-curb choice misidentifies what $l$ represents.

statement: A traffic engineer designs a signal with a yellow interval of $3.0 \text{ sec}$ for an approach with design speed $50 \text{ mph}$. Using $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, is this yellow time adequate?

choices.text: No -- the required yellow is 4.7 sec; using 3.0 sec creates a dilemma zone where drivers can neither stop nor clear the intersection
Yes -- 3.0 sec is the standard minimum yellow for all approach speeds
Yes -- the 3.0 sec yellow is adequate because drivers will slow down on approach
No -- but the shortfall can be made up by extending the all-red interval

explanation: Compute the required yellow: v = 50 x 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. y = 1.0 + 73.3/(2 x 10) = 1.0 + 3.67 = 4.67, approximately 4.7 sec. The actual yellow of 3.0 sec is 1.7 sec too short. This creates a "dilemma zone" -- a region where a driver is too close to stop safely but too far to clear the intersection during the yellow. This is a serious safety problem. The "3.0 sec is the standard minimum for all speeds" option is wrong because yellow time is speed-dependent. The "adequate because drivers will slow down" option assumes drivers slow down, but the design must accommodate the design speed. The "make up the shortfall with the all-red interval" option is wrong because the all-red serves a different purpose (clearance of vehicles already in the intersection, not stopping decisions).

statement: A freeway has free-flow speed $S_f = 60 \text{ mph}$ and jam density $D_j = 200 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. What is the optimum density at maximum flow?
explanation: At maximum flow, the optimum density is exactly half the jam density: $D_o = D_j/2 = 200/2 = 100$ veh/mi/ln. This comes straight from the Greenshields model. The choice 200 is the jam density itself, not the optimum. The choice 50 divides the jam density by 4 instead of 2. The choice 150 is three-quarters of the jam density, which has no significance in the model.

statement: In the Greenshields model, what happens to flow as density increases from zero toward jam density?

choices.text: Flow increases linearly until it reaches jam density
Flow increases to a maximum at half the jam density, then decreases back to zero
Flow remains constant regardless of density
Flow decreases monotonically from free-flow conditions to jam density

explanation: The Greenshields model produces a parabolic flow-density curve. At zero density, flow is zero (no cars). As density increases, flow rises to a peak at $D = D_j/2$, then falls back to zero at jam density (cars are bumper-to-bumper, speed = 0). The "increases linearly until jam density" option incorrectly assumes a linear relationship. The "flow remains constant" option ignores the speed-density tradeoff. The "decreases monotonically from free-flow to jam density" option describes a monotonically decreasing function, but flow actually starts at zero when there are no vehicles.

statement: An engineer computes the RMEV for two intersections. Intersection A has RMEV $= 3.5$ and Intersection B has RMEV $= 1.8$. The ADT at Intersection A is twice the ADT at Intersection B. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Intersection A has a higher crash rate per vehicle exposure, so it may warrant safety improvements first
Intersection A is safer because it carries more traffic
The two intersections cannot be compared because they have different ADTs
Intersection B is more dangerous because a lower RMEV means more severe crashes

explanation: RMEV already normalizes crashes by exposure (per million entering vehicles), so different ADTs are already accounted for. A higher RMEV means more crashes per million vehicles, regardless of total volume. Intersection A at 3.5 has nearly double the crash rate of B at 1.8, making it the stronger candidate for safety review. The "safer because it carries more traffic" choice confuses volume with safety. The "cannot be compared" choice is wrong because RMEV exists precisely to enable such comparisons. The "lower RMEV means more severe crashes" choice reverses the meaning of RMEV.

statement: A freeway segment has a free-flow speed of $110\,\text{km/h}$, 3 lanes per direction, and a peak-hour volume of 5400 vehicles. If the peak-hour factor (PHF) is 0.90, what is the peak 15-minute flow rate per lane?
explanation: The peak 15-min flow rate adjusts the hourly volume for the peaking within the hour: $V_p = V/(PHF \times N) = 5400/(0.90 \times 3) = 5400/2.7 = 2000$ veh/h/ln. The PHF accounts for the fact that traffic does not flow uniformly throughout the hour. Common trap is forgetting to divide by the number of lanes.

statement: On a freeway operating at Level of Service (LOS) F, which condition is most likely occurring?

choices.text: Stable flow with some speed reductions
Forced or breakdown flow with stop-and-go conditions

explanation: LOS grades go from A (best, free flow) to F (worst, breakdown). LOS F means demand exceeds capacity — you get queuing, stop-and-go traffic, and long delays. LOS A-C is good, D is approaching unstable, E is at capacity, F is breakdown. This is one of those definitions the FE loves to test.

statement: A freeway analysis produces a density of $34\,\text{pc/mi/ln}$. If the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor $f_{HV}$ was accidentally set to $1.0$ instead of its true value of $0.85$, what would happen to the computed density and LOS?

choices.text: The computed density would be lower than actual, potentially understating congestion
The computed density would be higher than actual, overstating congestion
Density would be unchanged because $f_{HV}$ only affects speed
The LOS would improve because passenger cars flow more smoothly

explanation: $f_{HV}$ appears in the denominator of $v_p = V/(PHF \times N \times f_{HV})$. If you set $f_{HV} = 1.0$ when it should be 0.85, the denominator gets bigger, making $v_p$ smaller. A smaller $v_p$ means a smaller density $D = v_p/S$, which could shift the LOS one or two grades better than reality. You would think the road is less congested than it actually is. The real-world effect of trucks is that they take up more road space, so ignoring their impact makes the analysis unconservative.

statement: In the AASHTO flexible pavement design, the drainage coefficient $m$ for base and subbase layers accounts for:

choices.text: The compaction level achieved during construction
The expected moisture conditions and quality of drainage, which reduce the effective structural contribution of granular layers
The traffic loading applied to each individual layer
The temperature susceptibility of asphalt layers

explanation: The drainage coefficient $m$ adjusts for how well water drains from the granular base and subbase layers. Poor drainage means water sits in the layer, weakening it and reducing its effective structural contribution. Values of $m < 1.0$ penalize layers with poor drainage; $m = 1.0$ means good drainage. The surface course (layer 1) always uses $m = 1.0$ by convention because asphalt is relatively impermeable. The compaction-level choice describes a construction quality issue, not drainage. The traffic-loading choice is captured by ESALs, not by m. The temperature-susceptibility choice applies to asphalt, not granular layers.

statement: Two pavement sections have the same required Structural Number ($SN = 4.0$). Section A uses a thicker asphalt surface with a thinner granular base. Section B uses a thinner asphalt surface with a thicker granular base. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Both designs are structurally equivalent per the SN equation, but Section A will likely perform better because asphalt has a higher layer coefficient than granular base
Section B is always the better design because granular base is less expensive
The two sections cannot have the same SN with different layer thicknesses
Section A is overdesigned because thicker asphalt exceeds the SN requirement

explanation: The SN equation allows different thickness combinations to reach the same total SN. Since asphalt has $a_1 = 0.44$ (much higher than granular base $a_2 = 0.14$), each inch of asphalt provides about 3 times the structural benefit of an inch of base. Section A with more asphalt gets the same SN with less total pavement thickness, and higher-quality materials on top generally provide better performance. Section B may be cheaper in materials but needs much more total thickness. Both satisfy the design SN, so they are structurally equivalent by the AASHTO method. The "granular base is always cheaper/better" choice ignores performance differences. The "cannot have the same SN with different thicknesses" choice misunderstands the SN equation. The "Section A is overdesigned" choice is wrong because both sections hit exactly $SN = 4.0$.

statement: Two cross sections are $50 \text{ ft}$ apart with areas $A_1 = 180 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 220 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the earthwork volume using the average end area method, in cubic yards?
explanation: $V = L(A_1 + A_2)/2 = 50(180 + 220)/2 = 50 \times 400/2 = 50 \times 200 = 10{,}000$ ft$^3$. Convert: $10{,}000/27 = 370$ yd$^3$. The 10,000 yd$^3$ option is in ft$^3$, not yd$^3$ -- forgot to divide by 27. The 741 yd$^3$ option forgot to divide by 2 in the average: $50 \times 400/27 = 741$. The 333 yd$^3$ option used only $A_1$: $50 \times 180/27 = 333$.

statement: The average end area method always overestimates the true volume compared to the prismoidal formula (when the two end areas are not equal). Why?

choices.text: The average end area method uses a larger distance $L$ than the prismoidal formula
The average end area method assumes a linear transition between the two cross sections, but the actual shape tapers, so the true mid-section area is smaller than the average of the two ends
The prismoidal formula ignores the mid-section, so it always underestimates
The overestimate occurs only when both areas are very large

explanation: The average end area method takes $(A_1 + A_2)/2$ as the representative cross section for the entire segment. But when $A_1$ and $A_2$ differ, the actual mid-section area $A_m$ is typically less than $(A_1 + A_2)/2$ because the cross section tapers non-linearly. The prismoidal formula accounts for this by weighting the mid-section $4\times$. Mathematically, $(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2)/6 \leq (A_1 + A_2)/2$ when $A_m < (A_1 + A_2)/2$, which is the typical case. The "larger distance $L$" choice is wrong -- both methods use the same $L$. The "prismoidal ignores the mid-section" choice is backwards -- the prismoidal formula uses $A_m$ and is more accurate. The "only when both areas are very large" choice is wrong because the overestimate depends on the difference between the areas, not their absolute size.

statement: A project has a cut section producing $5{,}000 \text{ yd}^3$ of excavation and a fill section requiring $5{,}000 \text{ yd}^3$ of embankment. An engineer assumes the cut material can directly fill the embankment with no waste or borrow. What critical factor has the engineer overlooked?

choices.text: Shrinkage and swell factors -- excavated soil changes volume when disturbed and recompacted, so equal bank volumes do not mean equal compacted volumes
The two sections may be different soil types, but volume is unaffected by soil type
The hauling cost, which is the only consideration in mass haul analysis
The average end area method was used, which always gives exact volumes

explanation: When soil is excavated, it expands (swells) because of loosening. When it is placed as fill and compacted, it shrinks below the original bank volume (shrinkage). So 5,000 yd$^3$ of bank cut does not produce 5,000 yd$^3$ of compacted fill. Depending on the soil, you might get only 4,250 yd$^3$ of compacted fill from 5,000 yd$^3$ of bank cut (about 15% shrinkage for typical clay). The engineer would need to borrow additional material. The "different soil types but volume unaffected" choice acknowledges soil differences but incorrectly claims volume is unaffected. The "hauling cost is the only consideration" choice ignores the volume balance issue. The "average end area always gives exact volumes" choice is wrong because that method overestimates, not gives exact volumes.

statement: Compared with flexible pavement, a rigid (PCC) pavement is generally LESS sensitive to subgrade strength. Why?

choices.text: The stiff slab distributes load over a wide area by beam action
Concrete is weaker in bending than asphalt
Rigid pavement transmits all load directly beneath the wheel

explanation: A rigid slab bends like a beam and spreads each wheel load over a large area of subgrade, so the foundation strength matters less than for flexible pavement. The "concrete is weaker in bending than asphalt" choice is false (concrete carries the bending). The "transmits all load directly beneath the wheel" choice is the opposite of slab behavior. The "rigid pavement has no subgrade" choice is incorrect — there is always a subgrade.

statement: Under the MUTCD, a green sign giving the distance to the next town is which category of traffic control device?
explanation: Green signs that give directions, distances, and destinations are GUIDE signs. Regulatory signs (white/red) state laws; warning signs (yellow diamonds) alert to conditions; a signal indication is a traffic light, not a sign.

statement: During the peak hour an approach records $2{,}400 \text{ veh/hr}$ with a peak 15-minute count of $700 \text{ veh}$. What is the peak hour factor (PHF)?
explanation: $PHF = V/(4 \times V_{15}) = 2{,}400/(4 \times 700) = 2{,}400/2{,}800 = 0.857$. The 0.292 option divided $V_{15}$ by $V$ and forgot the factor of 4 in the wrong place: $700/2{,}400 = 0.292$. The 1.167 option inverted the ratio: $2{,}800/2{,}400$. The 0.750 option used $V_{15} = 800$ by mistake. PHF is always between 0.25 and 1.00.

statement: A vertical curve is designed with a K-value of $K = 160$ connecting a $-2\%$ grade to a $+3\%$ grade. What is the required curve length $L$?
explanation: $A = |g_2 - g_1| \times 100 = |0.03 - (-0.02)| \times 100 = 0.05 \times 100 = 5$. Then $K = L/A$ rearranges to $L = K \times A = 160 \times 5 = 800$ ft. The 160 ft choice reported $K$ as if it were $L$. The 32 ft choice computed $K/A = 160/5$ instead of $K \times A$. The 320 ft choice used $A = 2$ (only one grade magnitude): $160 \times 2$.

statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 1{,}000 \text{ ft}$ and intersection angle $I = 40\degree$. What is the middle ordinate $M$?
explanation: $M = R[1 - \cos(I/2)] = 1{,}000[1 - \cos(20\degree)] = 1{,}000(1 - 0.9397) = 1{,}000 \times 0.0603 = 60.3$ ft. The 234 ft choice used $\cos(I) = \cos(40\degree) = 0.766$ instead of $\cos(I/2)$: $1{,}000(1 - 0.766) = 234$. The 64.2 ft choice is the external distance $E = R[1/\cos(I/2) - 1] = 1{,}000(1/0.9397 - 1) = 64.2$, not the middle ordinate. The 30.2 ft choice halved the correct answer.

statement: Two crosswalks have identical lengths and pedestrian speeds, but Crosswalk A serves $5$ pedestrians per cycle while Crosswalk B serves $25$. Using $G_p = 3.2 + L/S_p + 0.27 N_{\text{ped}}$, how does the required pedestrian green time compare?

choices.text: They are equal because the walking time term $L/S_p$ dominates the calculation
Crosswalk B requires about 5.4 sec more green time because the $0.27 N_{\text{ped}}$ term grows with pedestrian volume
Crosswalk B requires 5 times the green time of Crosswalk A
Crosswalk A requires more green time because fewer pedestrians walk more cautiously

explanation: The only term that differs between the two crosswalks is $0.27 N_{\text{ped}}$. The difference in that term is $0.27(25 - 5) = 0.27 \times 20 = 5.4$ sec, so B needs about 5.4 sec more. The start-up constant (3.2) and the walking time ($L/S_p$) are identical for both. The option that they are equal because the walking time term $L/S_p$ dominates the calculation is wrong because the volume term, while smaller, is not zero. The option that Crosswalk B requires 5 times the green time of Crosswalk A wrongly assumes green time scales linearly with pedestrian count -- only one of three terms depends on $N_{\text{ped}}$. The option that Crosswalk A requires more green time because fewer pedestrians walk more cautiously invents a behavior not in the formula.

statement: A freeway carries $20\%$ trucks ($P_T = 0.20$) on rolling terrain ($E_T = 3.0$). What is the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor $f_{HV}$?
explanation: $f_{HV} = 1/[1 + P_T(E_T - 1)] = 1/[1 + 0.20(3.0 - 1)] = 1/[1 + 0.20 \times 2] = 1/1.40 = 0.714$. The 0.625 distractor used $E_T = 3.0$ without subtracting 1: $1/[1 + 0.20 \times 3] = 1/1.60$. The 1.400 distractor reported the denominator itself instead of its reciprocal. The 0.600 distractor computed $1 - P_T \times E_T = 1 - 0.60$.

statement: Two freeway segments are analyzed. Segment 1 has a density of $24 \text{ pc/mi/ln}$ and Segment 2 has a density of $40 \text{ pc/mi/ln}$. Using the LOS density boundaries (A $\leq 11$, B $> 11$–18, C $> 18$–26, D $> 26$–35, E $> 35$–45, F $> 45$), which statement is correct?

choices.text: Segment 1 is LOS B and Segment 2 is LOS D
Segment 1 is LOS C and Segment 2 is LOS E
Both segments operate at LOS D
Segment 1 is LOS C and Segment 2 is LOS F

explanation: LOS is read directly from density. Segment 1 at 24 pc/mi/ln falls in the $> 18$ to $26$ band, which is LOS C. Segment 2 at 40 pc/mi/ln falls in the $> 35$ to $45$ band, which is LOS E. The 'LOS B / LOS D' choice shifts both grades one letter too good. The 'both at LOS D' choice wrongly lumps both into D. The 'LOS C / LOS F' choice pushes Segment 2 to F, but F only begins above 45 pc/mi/ln.

statement: An embankment requires $9{,}000 \text{ yd}^3$ of compacted fill. The borrow soil has a shrinkage factor such that compacted volume is $0.90$ times the bank (in-place) volume. How many cubic yards of bank material must be excavated from the borrow pit?
explanation: Compacted volume $= 0.90 \times$ bank volume, so bank volume $=$ compacted volume $/ 0.90 = 9{,}000/0.90 = 10{,}000$ yd^3. Soil shrinks when compacted, so you must dig MORE bank material than the finished fill volume. The 8,100 yd^3 option multiplied by 0.90 instead of dividing: $9{,}000 \times 0.90$. The 9,000 yd^3 option ignored shrinkage entirely. The 9,900 yd^3 option added 10% instead of dividing by 0.90.

statement: A zone produces $P_i = 800$ trips, distributed to two zones with weights $A_1 F_1 = 120$ and $A_2 F_2 = 80$ (K = 1). How many trips go to the first zone?
explanation: Fraction to zone 1 = 120/(120 + 80) = 120/200 = 0.60, so T = 800 × 0.60 = 480 trips. The 320 trips choice is the trips to zone 2 (80/200 × 800). The 400 trips choice splits evenly. The 120 trips choice reports the raw weight, not the trips.

statement: Which design parameter is used to characterize foundation support specifically in RIGID pavement design?
explanation: Rigid pavement design uses the modulus of subgrade reaction k (pressure per unit deflection) to describe how the subgrade supports the slab. The structural number (SN) is for flexible pavement; Marshall stability and penetration grade are asphalt-mix and binder properties.

statement: An engineer finds that an intersection does not meet any MUTCD signal warrant. What is the appropriate conclusion?

choices.text: A signal is not justified; installing one could worsen safety and delay
Install the signal anyway, since signals always help
Warrants do not apply to existing intersections
A signal must be installed to satisfy the MUTCD

explanation: If no warrant is met, a signal is not justified — installing one can increase rear-end crashes and cause unnecessary delay. The "install anyway" option wrongly assumes signals always help. The claim that warrants do not apply to existing intersections is false (warrants apply broadly). The "a signal must be installed" option inverts the purpose of a warrant analysis.

statement: Activity A has a duration of 5 days. Activity B depends on A (finish-to-start) and has a duration of 3 days. If A starts on day 0, what is the early finish of B?
explanation: A starts day 0, finishes day 5 ($ES = 0$, $EF = 0 + 5 = 5$). B starts when A finishes (FS), so $ES_B = 5$. $EF_B = 5 + 3 = 8$. Day 5 is EF of A, not B. Day 3 is just B's duration. Day 15 multiplied $5 \times 3$ instead of adding.

statement: In a CPM network, activity C has two predecessors: A (EF = 6) and B (EF = 9). Both relationships are finish-to-start. What is the early start of C?
explanation: When an activity has multiple predecessors (all FS), its $ES$ = the MAXIMUM of all predecessor EFs. C cannot start until BOTH A and B are done. $\max(6, 9) = 9$. The "Day 6" choice took the minimum — C can't start at day 6 because B isn't done yet. The "Day 15" choice added both EFs. The "Day 7.5" choice averaged them.

statement: In the same network, what is the late finish of activity B?
explanation: B feeds two successors: D ($LS_D = 7$) and E ($LS_E = 10$). The backward pass uses MIN: $LF_B = \min(7, 10) = 7$. B must finish by day 7 so that D can start on time.
